messages.content: The wheel on my cart has developed a crack in one of the spokes. Can I bind it with wire to get through harvest season?

A cracked spoke will fail under the stress of a loaded cart, and binding it with wire only hides the weakness without restoring strength. Replace the spoke now before it breaks completely and damages the hub or rim, which would require much more extensive repair. Continuing to use a wheel with cracked spokes risks losing your load or the entire wheel, possibly causing injury.
My lamp wick burns unevenly and smokes badly even though I trim it regularly. What causes this?

An uneven flame usually means the wick is clogged with carbon or the wick itself is of poor quality and twisted. Trim it straight across, not to a point, and if smoking persists despite proper trimming and flame height, replace the wick entirely. Also ensure your fuel is clean, as impurities will foul even a good wick.
The rope on my well bucket is starting to fray near the handle. Can I just keep using it?

No, replace that rope immediately before it fails and you lose the bucket or worse. A frayed section will only weaken further under load, and water buckets can be quite heavy when full. Inspect the entire length for other weak spots when you restring it.
My chisel edge is rounded over from use. Should I keep grinding or is it ruined?

A rounded edge simply needs proper reshaping on the grindstone — work carefully to restore the bevel angle, keeping the tool cool with frequent water dips. Grind until you reach fresh metal with a straight edge, then hone on your finest stone. The chisel has plenty of life remaining unless the steel itself is cracked or the tang is loose.
I need to fell a tree leaning heavily toward my shed. Should I try to pull it the other direction with ropes as I cut?

A tree already leaning holds tremendous weight that will overpower any rope you can rig, and it may split or twist unpredictably as it falls. This work is beyond what one should attempt without proper experience; get help from someone who knows how to manage a dangerous fall, or accept that the tree must come down where it leans and move what you can from its path.
My ladder has a cracked rung about halfway up. Can I just avoid stepping on that one?

Never use a ladder with any cracked or damaged rungs, as the break can spread suddenly or you may step there by habit or in haste. Replace the broken rung with sound wood of the same species and thickness, fitted and pinned securely, or stop using the ladder altogether. A fall from height can kill or cripple.
How do I know when my chisel is sharp enough?

A properly sharpened chisel will pare a thin shaving cleanly from end-grain wood without crushing the fibers. It should also shave hair from your arm with light pressure. If the edge tears wood or requires heavy force, return it to the stone.
The wick on my lantern keeps smoking no matter how I trim it. What's wrong?

Clean the chimney thoroughly, as soot buildup restricts air and causes smoking. Check that the wick is evenly trimmed and not charred unevenly, and ensure you are using proper lamp oil rather than contaminated or unsuitable fuel. Adjust the flame height lower if smoking persists—too high a flame for the chimney size will always smoke.
The rope on my pulley system has gone stiff and some of the outer strands are fraying badly. Can I still use it for lifting heavy loads?

Absolutely not—stiff, frayed rope has lost much of its strength and may fail without warning under load. Replace it entirely before attempting any further lifting, as a broken rope under tension can cause serious injury or death.
The grinding stone has a deep groove worn in it from my axe. Does this matter?

Yes, the groove will grind a corresponding hollow into any edge you sharpen there, weakening it. Dress the stone flat with a stone dresser or chisel, or reserve the grooved section for roughing work only and use an unworn area for finish grinding. A true, flat stone surface is essential for proper edge geometry.
How do I stop my axe handle from working loose in the head?

Drive a hardwood wedge into the top of the handle through the eye of the axe head, expanding the wood to fill the socket completely. Some add a thin cross-wedge of metal for extra security. If the handle has already shrunk badly from drying out, you may need to fit an entirely new handle rather than trying to tighten a poor fit.
The grindstone in our workshop wobbles badly when turning. My father says to just work carefully around it, but it makes me nervous.

A wobbling grindstone is dangerous and will produce uneven sharpening at best, or shatter and cause injury at worst. Stop using it immediately and check whether the axle is bent, the mounting holes are worn uneven, or the stone itself is cracked. Replace any damaged parts; a grindstone that cannot spin true is not safe to operate.
My drawknife blade keeps catching and tearing the grain instead of shaving smoothly. What am I doing wrong?

You are likely working against the grain direction. Reverse your stroke so the blade follows the grain downhill, and check that your edge is sharp enough to slice cleanly rather than dig. A dull drawknife will tear regardless of direction.
My saw keeps binding and wandering off the line partway through a cut. What causes this?

The teeth may have lost their set, causing the kerf to pinch the blade, or the saw plate may have developed a kink or bend. Check that the set is even on both sides and that the blade is straight when sighted down its length. Uneven set or a warped plate must be corrected before the saw will cut true.
My draw-knife blade has gone dull along one edge. Is it worth trying to sharpen it myself, or should I just keep using it as is?

A dull draw-knife will fight you at every stroke and may slip dangerously when it catches. Take it to a grindstone and restore the bevel carefully, keeping the angle true and the edge straight. A sharp blade cuts clean and safe; a dull one is neither use nor ornament.
The wooden handle on my sledge has a lengthwise crack running four inches up from the head. Can I wrap it with wire to keep using it?

Wire wrapping may seem to hold the crack closed but does nothing to restore the handle's strength—it will still fail suddenly under a hard blow, putting you at serious risk. Replace the handle entirely. A cracked handle on a heavy striking tool is extremely dangerous and should never be used.
My chisel edge keeps crumbling when I pare hardwood, even after I sharpen it. What's wrong?

The edge is likely ground to too acute an angle for the hardness of the wood, or the steel has lost its temper from overheating during grinding. Try increasing the bevel angle slightly for more support behind the edge. If the steel has been blued from heat, that portion is ruined and must be ground away before re-sharpening.
Can I use my wood-splitting axe to chop down a tree?

A splitting axe has a thick wedge meant to force wood apart along the grain, while felling requires a thinner blade that cuts across the grain. Use a proper felling axe for cutting trees; using the wrong tool dulls the edge quickly and makes the work harder and less safe.
My knife blade has a chip in the edge from hitting bone. Should I just sharpen around it or grind the whole edge back?

Grind the entire edge back past the chip to restore a continuous cutting line, even though this removes more metal. A chipped edge will catch and tear rather than cut cleanly, and the damaged spot creates a weak point that invites further breaking. Use the grindstone carefully to avoid overheating the blade.
My ladder has a cracked rung about halfway up. Is it safe to use if I just avoid stepping on that rung?

A cracked rung weakens the entire ladder and may fail unexpectedly, causing a fall. Replace the damaged rung with sound timber of the same thickness, properly fitted and fastened, or do not use the ladder at all until repaired.
My chisel edge is rounded over and won't cut square corners anymore. Can I just keep using it for rough work?

A rounded edge will split the wood fibers instead of severing them cleanly, causing tear-out even in rough work and making the chisel harder to control. Regrind the bevel on a stone until you restore a proper square edge, checking often against a try-square. A properly sharpened chisel works safer and faster than a dull one in any application.
My ladder has a cracked rung about halfway up. Is it safe to use if I just avoid stepping on that one rung?

Remove the ladder from service until the rung is properly replaced. A cracked rung indicates stress or aging, you may forget and step on it in haste, and the ladder's overall integrity is compromised.
I'm sharpening a drawknife and can't tell which bevel angle is correct.

A drawknife typically takes a bevel of about twenty-five to thirty degrees on the outer face only, with the inner face left flat. Match the angle already established if previous sharpening is visible, and test on scrap wood until it peels shavings cleanly without digging or skipping.
The wick in my oil lamp has gotten crusty and black at the top and barely gives any light now even when turned up.

Trim away the charred portion with scissors, cutting straight across to expose fresh wick. A blackened wick cannot draw oil properly and will smoke rather than give good light. Trim it each time it becomes encrusted, and keep the font filled so the wick draws fuel easily.
I stored my best plane in the shed over winter and now there's rust on the blade. How do I clean it off?

Light rust can be removed by rubbing with fine sand or ash on an oiled cloth, working along the length of the blade. For deeper rust, use a whetstone with oil, grinding carefully to restore a clean surface. Afterward, keep the blade lightly oiled and store the tool in a dry place to prevent recurrence.
My chisel edge has a small chip in it. Should I grind the whole edge back past the chip?

Yes, grind the entire edge back beyond the chip to reach sound metal, then reshape the bevel properly. A chipped edge will worsen with use and spoil your work. Take light passes on the grindstone and cool the tool frequently in water to prevent losing the temper of the steel.
My hatchet handle cracked near the eye. Can I bind it with wire and keep using it?

A cracked handle near the head is dangerous and cannot be safely repaired with wire or binding. The force of each swing weakens the wood further, and the head may fly loose and cause serious injury. Replace the handle entirely before using the hatchet again.
My draw-knife blade has gone dull and tears the wood instead of shaving it smooth. What should I do?

A draw-knife must be sharp to cut cleanly across the grain. Secure the blade and hone both bevels with a whetstone, maintaining the original angle, then strop the edge on leather. Test on scrap wood before returning to your work.
The wheel on my cart has started wobbling badly and makes a clacking sound with each turn. What should I check?

The hub is likely worn or the axle pin has loosened, allowing too much play in the wheel. Remove the wheel and inspect the axle hole in the hub for elongation or cracking, and check that the linchpin or retaining wedge is tight. If the hub itself is damaged, the wheel needs rebuilding or replacement—a wheel coming off under load can cause serious injury.
I need to sharpen my scythe before the hay is ready, but I've only got a coarse stone. Will that do the job?

A coarse stone alone will leave the edge too rough for clean cutting through grass. Use the coarse stone first to reshape any nicks or damage, then finish with a finer stone or whetstone to hone a smooth, sharp edge. Stroke along the curve of the blade at a shallow angle, keeping the motion consistent on both sides.
The iron rim on my cart wheel is loose. Can I just nail it back on?

Nailing will not work and may split the wooden felloes. The rim needs to be heated until expanded, fitted tightly onto the wheel, then cooled rapidly so it shrinks tight. This is skilled work requiring proper equipment and judgment—take the wheel to someone experienced in this task, as a rim that comes off while the cart is moving can cause serious upset.
My ladder has one cracked rung near the bottom. Should I just avoid stepping on that one?

Replace the cracked rung immediately; you may step on it by habit or in haste, and any cracked rung weakens the ladder's structure. A broken rung will fail suddenly and completely, giving no second chance. Repair it properly or remove the ladder from service until fixed.
My chisel edge is chipping when I strike it. What causes this and how do I fix it?

The edge is too thin, too hard from overheating during grinding, or you are cutting material too tough for the tool. Grind back past the damaged area to sound metal, reshape the bevel slightly thicker, and keep the steel cool while grinding. For very hard wood or knots, use a heavier chisel or different approach.
My auger bit wanders off-center when I start boring into hardwood.

Use a bradawl or sharp nail to create a starting dimple exactly where you want the hole, giving the center spur a positive seat. Begin turning with light pressure until the bit is well established, then apply fuller force. Check that your bit's center point is sharp and projects slightly beyond the cutting spurs.
The grindstone wobbles badly on its axle. Should I keep using it to sharpen my tools?

Never use a wobbling grindstone, as it may shatter and cause grave injury. Check whether the axle is bent or the mounting holes in the stone have worn oval-shaped. A bent axle must be straightened or replaced; if the stone itself is damaged, it cannot be safely repaired and you need a new one.
My handsaw keeps wandering off the line when I start a cut, no matter how carefully I mark it. What's the trick?

Start the cut with short, controlled strokes, guiding the blade with your thumbnail against the far side of the line until a shallow kerf is established. Keep the saw at a low angle and let the weight of the blade do the work; forcing it will cause it to wander. Once the kerf is deep enough to guide the blade, lengthen your strokes and maintain a steady rhythm.
The leather strop I use after honing seems to be rounding my blade edges. Am I stropping wrong?

You're likely using too much pressure or too many strokes, which allows the leather's give to curl the very apex of the edge. Strop with light pressure for just a few passes per side, keeping the blade flat to the bevel angle. The strop refines an already-sharp edge; heavy stropping undoes the crisp edge your stone created.
The wooden handle on my splitting maul has cracked near where it meets the head. Can I wrap it with wire to keep using it?

No, a cracked handle near the head will fail under the shock of splitting and the head may fly loose, causing serious injury. Replace the handle entirely with sound, straight-grained hickory or ash fitted properly to the eye. A temporary repair on a striking tool is never safe.
The wedge in my axe-head has loosened and the head shifts when I swing. How do I fix this?

A loose axe-head is dangerous and must be tightened immediately. Drive the wooden wedge deeper with a mallet, or if the wood has dried and shrunk too much, soak the head in water overnight to swell the timber, then re-drive or replace the wedge.
My crosscut saw keeps binding in the log even though I just set fresh teeth. What causes that?

Your set is likely uneven, causing the blade to drift and pinch, or insufficient, making the kerf too narrow. Check that teeth are bent equally on both sides and far enough to clear the blade thickness, and ensure you're not forcing the saw faster than the teeth can clear sawdust.
I want to sharpen my scythe but I've only got a coarse grinding wheel. Will that work?

The coarse wheel will remove metal quickly but leaves an edge too rough for clean cutting of grass or grain. After grinding the basic bevel, you must finish with a whetstone—a fine-grit stone kept wet while you work along the blade's length. Carry the stone in the field and touch up the edge throughout the day.
I'm cleaning my lamp chimney and it has a brown haze that won't wipe off. What should I use?

Soak the chimney in warm water with washing soda, then wipe with a cloth or crumpled newspaper. For stubborn carbon deposits, use a paste of wood ash and water, rubbing gently to avoid scratching. Rinse thoroughly and dry completely before placing back on the lamp.
My chisel edge went dull after hitting a hidden nail. Should I grind out the damage or just keep sharpening the edge as-is?

Grind back past the damaged section until you reach undamaged steel, then re-establish the bevel and hone as usual. Trying to sharpen over a chip or rolled edge wastes time and leaves a weak spot that will fail again under use.
Can I splice two different thicknesses of rope together for hoisting, using the thinner rope I have on hand?

Splicing different thicknesses creates a weak point that may fail under load — always match rope diameter closely. For hoisting, the splice also jams in pulleys and creates dangerous shock loads. Use uniform rope throughout, or replace the entire line.
I need to cut a deep mortise and my chisel keeps wandering to one side as I go deeper. How do I keep it straight?

Make your layout lines clear and pare the walls vertically first to establish guides, taking light cuts. Work from both ends toward the middle when going deep, and clear waste frequently so you can see your progress. A mortise chisel with its thick blade resists bending better than a bench chisel for this work.
My ladder has one rung that wobbles a bit. Is it safe if I just avoid stepping on that rung?

Replace or properly repair the rung before using the ladder again. In a moment of haste or emergency you will forget which rung is weak, and a loose rung indicates the joints may be failing elsewhere. A fall from height can kill or cripple—ladder integrity is not negotiable.
When I'm riving shingles, the froe keeps sticking partway through the bolt and I have to hammer it side to side to get it moving again.

You're likely working across the grain instead of with it—examine the end of your bolt and start the froe so it follows the natural grain lines. Also ensure your bolts are from straight-grained wood without knots, and that the wood is still green enough to split cleanly rather than fracture.
My grindstone has worn unevenly and now has a hollow in the middle. Can I reshape it myself or do I need a new stone?

You can dress the stone back to a true round surface using a special truing tool or a hard stone pick, working slowly and checking frequently with a straight edge. Turn the stone and work across its face to remove the high spots at the edges until the surface is even again. This wastes some stone thickness but restores proper grinding action—a stone can be trued several times before it becomes too small to use effectively.
The wooden wheel on my cart has a crack running along one of the spokes. Can I bind it with wire or should I do something else?

A cracked spoke will only worsen under load and may fail suddenly, throwing the wheel out of true or collapsing entirely. Replace the spoke if you have the skill, or take the wheel to someone who does. Wire binding is false economy that risks a breakdown far from help.
My scythe blade chatters and skips instead of cutting smoothly through the tall grass.

The blade likely needs both sharpening and proper peening to restore the thin cutting edge. Work the edge on a stone until keen, and check that the blade is properly tensioned and aligned with the snath so it rides at the correct angle to the ground.
When I'm using my drawknife to strip bark, it keeps digging in and gouging the wood underneath instead of taking smooth shavings.

You're likely cutting with the bevel facing down, which makes the blade dig in rather than ride along the surface. Flip it so the bevel faces upward and pull with controlled, angled strokes. Keep the blade sharp and adjust your grip to maintain a consistent shallow cut.
The rope on my well bucket is fuzzy and worn in one spot. How much longer will it last?

Replace it now before it fails; worn rope gives little warning before breaking and a falling bucket can injure someone below or be lost entirely. Inspect the entire length for other weak spots, as wear in one place often indicates age throughout. A new rope is far cheaper than the consequences of failure.
My ladder has one cracked rung near the bottom. Should I repair it or replace the whole ladder?

Replace the cracked rung entirely with sound wood of the same species and dimension, properly mortised and secured. Never trust a cracked rung, even if it seems firm—a failure high up could cause grave injury.
The rope on my well bucket is starting to fray near where it runs over the pulley. What should I do?

Replace the entire rope before it fails and you lose the bucket or worse. Inspect the pulley wheel for rough spots or splits that caused the wear, and smooth or replace it as needed so the new rope is not damaged in turn.
I'm sharpening my drawknife on a whetstone. Should I work the bevel on both sides equally?

A drawknife typically has a single bevel on one face with the other left flat or nearly so. Maintain the existing angle on the beveled side and keep the back flat, testing the edge on a scrap of wood. Sharpening both sides equally will ruin the tool's geometry.
My grindstone has developed a deep groove in the middle from repeated sharpening. Does this matter?

Yes, the groove prevents you from sharpening blades evenly and will create curved or uneven edges. You need to dress the stone by working a hard flat stone across the surface to wear down the high spots, or have someone with a proper truing tool restore it to flat. A true, even surface is essential for producing straight, properly shaped edges on your tools.
My pulley squeaks terribly under load. Should I grease the axle pin?

Yes, but first inspect the sheave for cracks and ensure the pin isn't bent or worn thin where it bears the load. Clean out any grit, apply tallow or grease to the bearing surfaces, and verify the pulley isn't overloaded beyond its safe capacity.
The wheel on my cart wobbles badly and the iron tire is loose. What's the proper fix?

The wooden wheel has likely shrunk from drying out. A wheelwright should remove the tire, add wood segments to restore the rim's diameter, then heat and refit the tire so it contracts tightly as it cools. Attempting to use it loose will damage both tire and wheel beyond economical repair.
I left my saw outside and now there's surface rust on the blade. How do I clean it without ruining the set of the teeth?

Rub the rust away with fine sand or ash mixed with a little oil, working along the length of the blade and avoiding hard pressure on the teeth. Once clean, wipe the blade with an oiled rag to prevent future rust. Check that the set of the teeth remains even; if rust has pitted the metal deeply, the saw may need professional refiling.
My wood plane blade chatters and tears the grain no matter how I adjust it. What am I doing wrong?

The iron is likely dull or seated improperly in the bed. Sharpen it thoroughly on your stone until it takes a fine edge, then set it firmly with the cap iron just back from the edge to dampen vibration. Check also that the sole of the plane is flat and the mouth opening suits the cut you want.
Is it alright to store my good plane in the unheated workshop through winter?

Cold itself will not harm the plane, but dampness in an unheated space will cause rust on the blade and iron parts. Coat all metal surfaces with a light oil and store the tool where air can circulate around it. Check it periodically and re-oil if needed.
The rope on my well bucket is getting fuzzy and worn where it runs over the pulley wheel. Should I just turn it around so a different section takes the wear?

Inspect the entire length carefully first—if the wear is only surface fibers, turning it may help temporarily. However, if you can see into the inner strands or feel soft spots, the rope is no longer safe and must be replaced entirely. A broken well rope can mean injury or loss of your bucket deep in the well.
Is it safe to use a file that has some teeth broken off along one edge?

A file with broken teeth will still cut on the intact portions, though it works less evenly. Keep using it for rougher work where precision matters less, but obtain a sound file for finish work where you need consistent results across the full face.
The wick on my lamp burns unevenly and smokes. What's wrong?

The wick is likely charred unevenly or the lamp needs cleaning. Trim the wick straight across, removing all charred portions, and clean soot from the chimney and burner. If smoking continues with a proper flame height, the oil quality may be poor.
The wooden rungs on my ladder have dark cracks running along the grain. Is this just weathering?

Those cracks compromise the strength of the rungs and the ladder is no longer safe for use. Wood fails along the grain, and a cracked rung may break entirely under load. Replace the damaged rungs with sound wood of the same species and dimensions, or retire the ladder.
My axe head keeps coming loose from the handle when I split wood. What should I do?

The wood has likely dried and shrunk. Soak the head end of the handle in water overnight to swell the wood, then drive a hardwood wedge into the top of the handle through the eye. If the handle is cracked or badly worn, replace it entirely rather than risk the head flying off.
My plane blade chatters and leaves ripples in the wood instead of smooth shavings. How do I fix this?

Chatter usually means the blade is not seated firmly or is set too deep. Check that the wedge holds the blade tight without movement, adjust the blade to take a finer cut, and ensure the edge is sharp. Plane with the grain in steady, even strokes.
I'm trying to true up a wooden cartwheel that's developed a noticeable wobble. What's the best way to identify which spoke or section needs adjustment?

Spin the wheel slowly and hold a fixed pointer—a stick or your finger—close to the rim to see where it runs out of round. Check each spoke for tightness in its mortise and examine the felloe sections for cracks or loosened joints. Often the iron tire has simply loosened and needs to be heated, shrunk back onto the rim, and quenched to restore proper tension.
My ladder has a cracked rung about halfway up. Can I bind it with rope and keep climbing on it?

Do not trust your weight to a cracked rung even if bound, as it will fail suddenly. Replace the damaged rung with sound wood of the same species and diameter, ensuring the joints are tight. Until properly repaired, do not use that ladder for any work above ground.
My axe blade keeps sliding sideways in the handle when I strike. The wedge at the top looks tight enough.

The wedge may appear seated but the wood of the handle has likely shrunk from drying, or the eye of the head has widened from repeated impact. Drive the wedge deeper with a hammer, or if it bottoms out, remove it and fit a larger wedge cut from seasoned hardwood. Soak the head in linseed oil overnight to swell the wood fibers before re-wedging.
The wooden wheel on my cart has several spokes that wobble loose in their mortises. How do I tighten them properly?

Loose spokes will quickly destroy the wheel through uneven loading. Drive small hardwood wedges into the mortises alongside each loose spoke, or if the mortises have enlarged too much, remove the spokes and wrap their tenons tightly with linen strips soaked in hide glue before reinserting them. If more than half the spokes are loose, the hub itself may be split and the wheel should be rebuilt entirely.
My lamp smokes terribly and blackens the glass. Am I filling it too full?

Black smoke means the wick is too high or needs trimming—the flame should be steady and clean-burning, not reaching up to smoke. Trim the wick evenly across and adjust the height until the flame is bright but does not smoke. Also ensure you are burning proper lamp oil, as poor fuel will smoke regardless of wick adjustment.
My chisel edge crumbles when I use it on oak. Is the wood too hard?

Oak is not too hard for a properly tempered chisel; the edge is likely damaged from overheating during sharpening or from striking something metal. Grind back past all the crumbled metal to where the edge is sound, then resharpen carefully without letting it turn blue from heat. Keep water nearby when grinding to cool the steel frequently.
The rope on my well pulley is starting to fray near where it runs over the wheel. Should I wait until it breaks to replace it?

Replace frayed rope immediately, before it fails—a breaking rope could drop the bucket or injure someone below. Inspect the entire length for wear, and check that the pulley wheel is smooth and turning freely. A new rope is far cheaper than the consequences of a broken one.
My kitchen knife won't take an edge anymore even after honing. The steel seems soft. What should I do?

The blade has likely lost its temper through overheating or poor initial treatment and cannot be restored to proper hardness. Replace the knife rather than struggling with a blade that will not hold an edge. Proper knives should maintain sharpness through many honings when treated correctly.
The wheel on my cart wobbles badly and the iron tire is coming loose. How do I fix this properly?

The wheel may have dried out, causing the felloes to shrink and loosen the tire. Soak the wheel thoroughly in water to swell the wood, then have a smith heat the tire and reset it while hot so it contracts tight upon cooling. If the wobble comes from a damaged hub or loose spokes, the wheel needs rebuilding by someone skilled in wheelwrighting.
How do I know when my grindstone is too worn down to use safely?

A grindstone becomes dangerous when it is worn unevenly with grooves or flat spots, or when it becomes too small in diameter and spins too fast for its strength. Replace it when deep grooves form, when cracks appear, or when it is ground down to half its original thickness. A stone that flies apart can cause terrible injury.
My chisel edge has a small chip in it. How do I fix this?

Grind the edge back past the chip on the grindstone until you reach sound metal with no defects, then re-establish the bevel angle. This will shorten the chisel slightly, but a sound edge is essential for safe controlled cuts. Finish with a fine stone to restore a keen edge.
The ladder I use to reach the loft has a cracked rung about halfway up. It still holds my weight if I step lightly. Should I worry?

Replace that rung immediately or stop using the ladder altogether. A cracked rung can give way suddenly and completely, even under weight it previously supported. No repair short of full replacement is trustworthy for a structural member that must bear a person's weight.
The wick in my lamp burns black smoke and the glass is sooty. Is this just how oil lamps work?

A properly trimmed wick and clean oil burn with minimal smoke. Trim the wick to an even quarter-inch, clean the soot from the glass, and check that your oil is not contaminated with debris. The flame should be steady and yellow, not smoking or flickering wildly.
The wheel on my cart wobbles badly. What causes this and how do I fix it?

The hub may be worn, the axle bent, or the wheel spokes loose. Remove the wheel and examine the axle for straightness and the hub for play. Tighten any loose spokes and check that the wheel sits square on the axle; if the hub or axle is damaged beyond adjustment, have them repaired or replaced by someone with the proper tools.
I'm sharpening my chisel on the grindstone and the edge keeps turning blue from the heat. Does that matter?

That blue coloring means you've overheated the steel and destroyed its temper—the edge will no longer hold sharpness properly. Grind past all the discolored metal until you reach bright steel again, and work more slowly with lighter pressure and frequent water cooling. A ruined temper cannot be restored without a forge and proper heat treatment.
The wooden handle on my sledgehammer has a long crack running with the grain. Can I wrap it tightly with wire to hold it together?

Wire wrapping may seem to secure it, but a cracked handle can still fail suddenly under the shock of striking, sending the head flying or causing you to lose control. The handle must be replaced entirely. A sledgehammer generates tremendous force and a structural crack makes it dangerous to use.
I need to cut through a thick oak beam but my saw keeps binding and getting stuck partway through the cut.

The kerf is closing behind the blade as you cut, which happens with thick timber under tension. Drive a thin wooden wedge into the cut behind the saw to hold it open as you progress. Keep the saw sharp and cut with steady, full strokes rather than short jabs.
The rope on my well bucket is getting fuzzy and weak-looking in spots. Is there a way to make it last longer or should I replace it now?

A rope that shows worn or fuzzy sections cannot be trusted with a loaded bucket—it will part without warning. Replace it before it fails and sends your bucket into the depths. A new rope is a small cost compared to losing your bucket or the injury from a sudden break.
The rope on my well-bucket is starting to fray near the knot. How much fraying is too much?

Any fraying that exposes the inner strands is too much when the rope bears a load you cannot afford to drop. Inspect the entire length, for wear at one point often means hidden wear elsewhere. Replace the rope entirely, as a bucket lost down a well costs far more than new line.
The rope on my well pulley has worn smooth and shiny where it bends over the wheel. Is it still safe?

Smooth glazed sections indicate the fibers have been crushed and weakened by friction and load. Inspect closely for broken strands within the lay of the rope; if you find any, or if the rope has lost more than a quarter of its original thickness at the worn spot, replace it entirely. A parted rope under load has injured many, so err toward caution.
How deep should I set my plane iron to get the smoothest finish on this oak board?

Set the iron for the thinnest shaving that will still cut continuously — a shaving you can see through is ideal. Too deep a cut tears the grain and leaves ridges; adjust by tapping the iron back until you get whisper-thin curls. A sharp blade and light passes produce far better results than forcing heavy cuts.
What is the right way to store edge tools so they stay sharp?

Keep edge tools dry, lightly oiled, and separated so blades do not contact each other or hard surfaces. Hang them individually or wrap edges in leather or cloth. Moisture and metal-on-metal contact are the enemies of a keen edge.
The wheel on my barrow wobbles badly because the axle hole has worn oval. Can I pack it with grease and washers to tighten it up?

Packing a worn bearing is false economy that will leave you stranded when it fails under a full load. Replace the wheel hub or bore it out true and fit a proper bushing. A barrow is only useful when it runs straight and carries weight reliably.
I need to fell a large tree near my cottage but have only felled small ones before. What precautions matter most?

Clear all brush and plan two escape paths away from the tree at angles, never directly behind. Cut your notch on the side where you want the tree to fall, then saw from the opposite side slightly higher, leaving a hinge of wood to control the fall. If the tree is large enough that you doubt your judgment of its lean or your ability to place it safely, seek someone experienced—a badly directed fall can kill.
When I'm splitting wood with my axe, the head sometimes glances off instead of biting in. What am I doing wrong?

You're likely striking at the wrong angle or hitting knots and grain irregularities. Aim for cracks or the outer edge of the round where the grain is straighter, and swing so the bit meets the wood squarely, not at a sliding angle. Read the wood's grain before each stroke and adjust your aim—forcing a poor angle wastes effort and risks a dangerous deflection.
When I'm splitting kindling with my hatchet, should I strike down onto a chopping block or hold the wood in the air?

Always use a solid chopping block and keep your free hand well clear of the target. Holding small pieces invites a glancing blow straight into your fingers. For very small kindling, stand pieces upright on the block and strike with control.
One spoke in my cart wheel has split lengthwise but is still in place. Can I wrap it with wire to hold it together?

A split spoke has lost its strength and will fail completely under load, potentially causing the wheel to collapse while the cart is in use. Wire wrapping cannot restore structural integrity and may hide progressive failure until catastrophic collapse occurs. Replace the spoke properly, or have a wheelwright do it if you lack the skills, before putting any load on that wheel.
The rope on our well bucket is starting to fray near the knot. Can I just tie it shorter and keep using it?

No, that fraying indicates the rope fibers are breaking down and the damage likely extends beyond what you can see. Replace the entire rope before it fails—a bucket falling back down the well creates danger and can be difficult to retrieve. Inspect all working ropes regularly and retire them at the first sign of serious wear.
The leather on my strop is getting glazed and shiny. Does this matter for maintaining my edge?

A glazed strop has lost its ability to hold the fine abrasive compound and will simply burnish the edge rather than refining it. Roughen the leather with a stiff brush or coarse cloth, then reapply stropping compound, working it well into the surface. If the leather is too hardened or slick, replace it with fresh leather.
The ladder I use to reach the loft has one rung that feels slightly loose. Can I tighten it somehow?

A loose rung indicates failed joints that will only worsen with use, risking a fall. Replace the rung properly by drilling out the old one and fitting a new piece with sound mortises, or retire the ladder if the side rails themselves have weakened.
The wooden handle on my sledge has a lengthwise crack near the head. Can I bind it with wire and keep using it?

No, a cracked handle will fail without warning and cause serious injury. Replace the handle entirely—wood that has split along the grain has lost its strength and no amount of binding will restore it safely.
My grindstone has worn unevenly and now has a groove in it. Does this matter?

Yes, a grooved stone will produce an uneven bevel and ruin your edge. Dress the stone with a harder abrasive or a special tool to restore a flat, even surface. Keep the stone true by moving your work across its full width when sharpening.
My broadaxe blade is loose in the eye. Should I soak the whole head in water?

Soaking can swell the wood temporarily but it will shrink again when dried, making the problem worse. Drive a proper wooden wedge into the handle end from the top of the eye, and add a cross wedge if needed. If the handle has shrunk too much, it must be replaced with one properly fitted to the eye.
My drawknife keeps digging in too deep and gouging the work. Am I holding it wrong?

You must adjust both your angle of attack and the evenness of your pull. Present the blade at a slicing angle rather than straight down, and draw with steady pressure from both handles at once. If one side digs regardless of your hold, the edge may be ground unevenly and wants truing on the stone.
The rope I use for hauling has started showing fuzzy worn spots in several places along its length. Is it still safe for heavy loads?

Fuzzy worn areas indicate the outer fibers are breaking down, which weakens the rope significantly even if the core seems intact. Such rope might hold for light work but could fail suddenly under heavy strain. For safety in hauling or any work where failure means danger or loss, replace it with sound rope and retire the worn one to lighter duties like bundling.
My whetstone has become uneven with a hollow in the middle. Does this matter?

Yes, a dished stone will round your edges instead of keeping them straight and true. Flatten it by rubbing against a flat stone slab with coarse sand and water between them, checking progress frequently with a straightedge.
My cook stove draws poorly and fills the room with smoke. The chimney seems clear when I look up it.

Check that the damper is fully open and that no ash has built up beneath the grate, blocking air from below. A chimney may appear clear yet have creosote coating the walls, narrowing the flue—this requires sweeping with a brush. Also ensure the chimney top is higher than the roof peak and free of bird nests or debris, as poor draft often starts at the outlet.
I nicked the blade of my draw knife on a nail hidden in some old timber. There's a small chip taken out of the edge. Can I keep using it like this?

That chip will catch and tear the wood fibers rather than shaving them cleanly. Grind the edge back past the damaged section, reshaping the bevel carefully to maintain the original angle. The blade will be slightly narrower, but it will cut properly again.
How often should I oil my saw blades?

Wipe your saw with an oiled rag after each use to prevent rust, especially in damp conditions. A light coating is sufficient—too much oil will attract dust and gum up the blade. Store saws in a dry place and check them regularly for any spots of rust to address immediately.
The wheel on my cart wobbles badly. Can I pack the hub with grease to steady it?

Grease will not fix a wobble, which comes from a worn hub, loose spokes, or a damaged axle. Check that the spokes are tight in their mortises, the hub is not cracked, and the axle is straight and properly fitted. Repair or replace damaged parts rather than attempting to mask the problem.
My grindstone has developed a deep groove in the middle from repeated sharpening in the same spot. Does this matter?

Yes, a grooved stone will grind uneven bevels and ruin your edges. Dress the stone by grinding its surface flat again with a harder abrasive or a stone dresser, and in future move your tools across the full width of the wheel. A flat, true surface is essential for proper sharpening.
When I sharpen my chisel on the grindstone, I sometimes see tiny cracks appearing near the cutting edge and blue discoloration on the metal.

You are overheating the steel by grinding too hard or too long without cooling, which draws the temper and makes the edge brittle and prone to cracking. Keep a pan of water at hand and dip the chisel frequently to keep it cool throughout sharpening. If the edge has already turned blue, grind back past the discolored metal and work more gently.
My ladder has one rung that's cracked halfway through on one side. The other side is still solid. Is it safe to keep using if I'm careful?

No—that rung will fail without warning when you put your weight on it, likely when you're at a height where a fall would cause serious harm. Remove and replace that rung completely before using the ladder again, even for light work.
The wooden handle on my adze is splitting near where it enters the eye. How do I fix it?

A split handle can break completely under the shock of use, sending the head flying. Replace the handle entirely rather than attempting repairs—the stresses involved make this a matter of safety, not mere convenience.
I'm sharpening a chisel on the grindstone and the edge keeps turning blue. What does that mean?

The blue color shows you've overheated the steel and drawn out its temper, making it too soft to hold an edge. Grind past the discolored portion to reach good steel again, and work more slowly with lighter pressure and frequent cooling in water.
My axe head wobbles on the handle. Can I just wedge something in there to tighten it?

A loose axe head is dangerous and must be fixed properly. Drive a wooden wedge into the top of the handle where it passes through the eye, then soak the head in water overnight to swell the wood for a firm fit. If the handle itself is cracked or worn thin, replace it entirely rather than risk the head flying off during use.
My bucksaw blade bends to one side when I cut. Should I twist the frame tighter to straighten the blade's path?

A blade that wanders usually means uneven tooth set or uneven sharpening, not loose tension. Check that teeth are bent equally left and right along the blade's length, and that their points form an even line. Overtightening the frame may snap the blade or distort the frame itself.
My lamp wick keeps smoking and the glass is black. I trimmed it but it still smokes.

The wick needs proper shaping—trim it level and slightly round the corners rather than leaving it square-cut. Make sure the wick is not raised too high above the burner, and check that you're burning clean oil without impurities. If the burner holes are clogged with carbon, clean them with a fine wire.
There's a chip in the edge of my best chisel. Can I just grind past it or should I work around it?

Grind the edge back past the chip until you reach sound metal, maintaining the proper bevel angle throughout. A chipped edge will never cut cleanly and the damage may spread with use, ruining more of the blade. Take your time on the stone and keep the tool cool to preserve the temper.
My axe head keeps coming loose on the handle. I've tried wedging it tighter but it works free after a few swings. What should I do?

The wood has likely dried and shrunk since the head was fitted. Soak the axe head in water overnight to swell the wood, then drive in a proper wedge across the grain while it's expanded. If the handle itself is split or the eye is badly worn, fit a new handle entirely rather than risk the head flying free.
The rope I use for hauling has a few strands frayed in one spot. Can I still trust it for heavy loads?

Frayed strands indicate the rope is weakening and should not be trusted for heavy loads or any critical use. The damaged section will continue to deteriorate and may fail suddenly under strain. Retire the rope from heavy service, cut away the damaged section for lighter tasks, or replace it entirely.
I'm sharpening my chisel on the grindstone but one side of the edge is getting ground away more than the other, making it crooked.

You're applying uneven pressure or holding the tool at an angle to the stone's face. Keep the chisel flat against the stone and use both hands to guide it steadily across the full width of the wheel. Turn the stone slowly and let the abrasive do the work rather than pressing hard on one side.
My axe head keeps flying off the handle during use. Can I just hammer it back on tighter?

The wood has likely dried and shrunk, loosening the fit. Soak the head end of the handle in water overnight to swell the wood, then drive a hardwood wedge crosswise through the eye to secure it properly. If the handle is cracked or the eye is badly worn, replacement is the only safe remedy.
The wooden ladder I use for the barn has a cracked rung about halfway up. Can I just avoid stepping on that one?

A cracked rung makes the entire ladder unsafe and unreliable, as you may step there by habit or in haste. Replace the damaged rung with sound wood of the same thickness, properly fitted and secured. Your life depends on the ladder holding, so repair it completely before climbing again.
I dropped my good knife and now there's a chip broken out of the edge near the tip. Can I just sharpen past it?

You'll need to grind the entire edge back beyond the chip to restore a continuous cutting surface, which will take considerable time on the stone. Work the whole blade evenly to maintain its shape, removing metal slowly to avoid overheating and spoiling the temper. The knife will be narrower afterward but fully serviceable.
My saw blade wanders off the line when I'm cutting thick oak planks. What can I do to keep it straight?

Check that your saw teeth are evenly set on both sides—uneven set will pull the blade to one side. Make sure your kerf is wide enough for the blade to move freely, and start with shallow scoring cuts to establish a clean groove before cutting deeper. Keep your stance and arm motion aligned with the cut line rather than forcing the blade back on course.
When sharpening my drawknife, should I maintain the bevel on both sides or just one?

Most drawknives are beveled on one side only, with the other side left flat or nearly flat, allowing the flat face to ride against the work for controlled cuts. Maintain the existing bevel and keep the back flat. Putting a bevel on both sides changes the tool's geometry and makes it much harder to control.
When I use my drawknife the blade keeps chattering and tearing the wood instead of slicing clean.

The edge is likely dull or you're working against the grain. Sharpen the blade to a keen edge and observe the wood's grain direction, always pulling the knife so it slices with the grain rather than lifting it. Adjust your angle of attack—too steep an angle causes digging and tearing, while too shallow skates without cutting.
I'm cutting dovetails for a chest and the saw keeps wandering off my marked line, even though I'm being careful to follow it.

Your saw likely has uneven set in the teeth, causing it to pull to one side. Examine the teeth closely and use a saw set to correct any that are bent more than their neighbors. Also ensure you're starting the cut with proper form—let the weight of the saw do the work rather than forcing it.
The leather strop I use for my straight razor has gone hard and shiny in the middle. Should I throw it out?

Rough the hardened surface lightly with fine sandpaper to open the leather, then work in neat's-foot oil or tallow and let it absorb overnight. A strop can be restored many times before the leather wears through.
I'm trying to plane a board smooth but the blade keeps chattering and leaving ridges instead of taking clean shavings.

Your blade is likely dull, set too deep, or not seated firmly in the plane body. Sharpen the iron properly, then set it to take a very fine shaving—you should see a thin curl, not chunks. Ensure the wedge holds everything tight, and plane with the grain, not against it.
When I'm riving shingles from a cedar bolt, about half of them come out twisted no matter how I split them. What am I doing wrong?

Twisted grain in the bolt itself causes this. Sight along the bark before you begin and choose sections where the grain runs straight and true. Even good cedar will have spiral grain in some growth, which cannot be riven cleanly.
The wheel on my cart wobbles as it turns. I've checked and the axle pin is still in place.

The hub has likely worn loose on the axle from use, or the wheel's joints have worked apart. Remove the wheel and examine where wood meets metal—you may need to fit a shim or bushing to take up the play, or the wheel may need rebuilding if the spokes have loosened. A wobbling wheel will only worsen and may collapse under load.
The wheel on my cart wobbles badly but the axle pin looks fine. What should I check?

The hub bore has likely worn oval or the wooden wheel itself has loosened at the spokes. Tap the iron tire to check if it's loose, and examine where spokes meet the hub and rim for cracks or movement. A wheelwright should repair structural wheel damage before the wobble causes complete failure.
The grindstone wobbles on its axle. Should I pack the hole with rags to steady it?

Packing the axle hole creates uneven rotation that will worsen the wobble and may crack the stone during use. The axle hole needs proper bushing with fitted wood or metal, or the stone should be replaced if the hole has worn too large. A wobbling stone cannot sharpen evenly and poses risk of breaking.
When I chisel across the grain the wood keeps splitting ahead of where I'm cutting. What am I doing wrong?

You are likely cutting too deep in a single pass or angling the bevel downward into the work. Take shallower cuts and keep the bevel facing up so the chisel rides toward the surface rather than diving deeper. For cross-grain work, scoring the edges of your cut with a knife first will also prevent splitting beyond your layout lines.
The wooden handle on my hammer has a crack running halfway through. Should I wrap it with wire to keep using it?

No, replace the handle entirely. A cracked handle can break during a swing, causing you to lose control of the hammerhead with risk of injury. Wrapping will not restore strength and gives false confidence in a dangerous tool.
My axe head keeps working loose from the handle when I'm splitting wood. I've tried wedging it tighter but it still shifts after a few swings.

The wood of your handle has likely dried and shrunk since it was fitted. Soak the head in water overnight to swell the wood temporarily, then drive in a new wooden wedge across the grain of the handle, and follow with a metal wedge if you have one. If the handle itself is cracked or the eye of the axe is badly worn, replace the handle entirely rather than risk the head flying off.
My lamp wick keeps smoking and the glass chimney turns black within an hour. What needs adjusting?

The wick is likely turned up too high, starving the flame of air and producing incomplete combustion. Turn the wick down until the flame is steady and bright without smoking, and ensure the chimney is seated properly to create the correct draft. Trim any charred or uneven portions from the top of the wick.
The ladder rung feels slightly loose when I step on it. Is it still safe if I'm careful?

A loose rung is never safe regardless of caution, as it may give way suddenly under your weight. Remove the ladder from service immediately and repair it by re-seating the rung properly with new glue and wedges, or by replacing the rung entirely. Test all rungs firmly before returning the ladder to use.
I need to move a heavy barrel up a ramp into the loft. Can I just push it up if I get a good running start?

Never rely on momentum alone for heavy loads on a ramp—if you stumble or the barrel shifts, it will roll back over you. Rig a rope to the barrel and run it through a pulley anchored above, or have a second person holding a safety line behind. Steady controlled pulls are safer than one desperate shove.
The wheel on my cart is starting to crack around the hub. How long can I keep using it?

Cracks around the hub will spread with each load and rotation until the wheel fails completely, likely when you are far from home or carrying a heavy load. Replace the wheel now while you can choose the time and place, rather than waiting for it to break and leave you stranded or cause an accident. Wood wheels cannot be trusted once cracking begins at the hub.
I'm cutting a mortise with mallet and chisel, but the wood keeps splitting beyond where I want the cut to go, ruining the joint.

You're likely trying to remove too much wood at once or cutting too close to your layout lines without proper relief. Work from the center of the mortise outward in thin layers, leaving a small margin from your lines until the last careful paring cuts. Ensure your chisel is truly sharp, and strike with controlled blows rather than heavy force that drives splits into the surrounding wood.
Can I use my wood chisel to scrape old paint and mortar? It seems like it would work well.

No, using a wood chisel on paint or mortar will ruin the fine edge and may chip or crack the blade. Keep your chisels only for woodworking where their sharpness is needed. Use a scraper or old knife for rough work like paint removal.
My stove door doesn't seal well anymore and smoke leaks out around the edges. Is this dangerous?

Yes, smoke leaking into your dwelling is harmful to breathe and indicates the door has warped or the seal has deteriorated. Adjust the hinges and latch if possible, and replace any damaged gasket material with rope or clay as appropriate to your stove. If the door itself is badly warped or cracked, it must be repaired or replaced.
What is the proper angle for sharpening a chisel meant for fine joinery work?

A bevel of twenty-five to thirty degrees gives a fine chisel enough strength to resist folding while keeping the edge keen enough for clean paring cuts. Maintain the angle consistently across the width and polish the back flat for best results.
The rope on my well bucket is getting fuzzy and worn in spots. When should I replace it before it breaks?

Replace the rope when you see broken fibers, significant fuzzing, or any spots worn thin—don't wait until you see the inner core or until it feels weak. A rope supporting weight overhead must be completely sound, as a broken bucket line can cause injury and leaves you without water. Inspect the full length regularly, especially where it passes over the pulley.
The grinding wheel has a groove worn into it from sharpening scythes in the same spot. Does this matter?

A deep groove prevents proper contact and makes it nearly impossible to maintain the correct bevel angle. Either true the stone with a dressing tool to restore a flat surface, or replace the wheel if it's worn too thin to dress safely.
How often should I oil the wheel hubs on my cart?

Oil the hubs whenever you notice the wheel turning less freely or hear squeaking, and always after the cart has been through water or mud. Wipe away old grease and grit before applying fresh oil or tallow to the axle and hub. Regular attention prevents the wood from drying and splitting and keeps the iron from seizing.
The rope on our well pulley has become stiff and some of the strands are fraying badly near where it runs over the wheel.

Replace the rope entirely before it fails under load and causes injury or loss of the bucket. Inspect the pulley wheel for rough spots, splinters, or uneven wear that may have damaged the rope, and smooth or replace it as needed. A frayed rope cannot be trusted for lifting water or any weight.
My grindstone has developed a hollow in the middle from repeated use. How do I flatten it?

Dress the stone using a harder abrasive block or another piece of coarse stone, working in crossing patterns until the surface runs true again. Some craftsmen use a metal star-wheel dresser for this purpose. A hollow stone will ruin your tool bevels by creating rounded edges, so regular truing is essential maintenance.
My axe handle has a long crack running with the grain. Can I bind it with wire and keep using it?

A cracked handle will fail without warning under load, and binding with wire offers no real strength. Replace the handle entirely before use — a broken handle mid-swing can cause serious injury. Any axe work demands a sound, uncracked shaft.
The chisel edge chips easily even though I just sharpened it. What's the problem?

Chipping usually means the edge was ground too thin or the steel overheated during sharpening, which draws the temper and softens it. Grind a slightly thicker bevel and work slowly at the stone to keep the metal cool, dipping frequently in water. A properly tempered edge holds up to hard wood without crumbling.
I need to lift a heavy beam. Can I double up two ropes side by side through the pulley to make them stronger?

Doubling ropes that way does not reliably double the strength, as one rope often takes more load than the other, and they can bind or slip unevenly. Use a single rope of adequate thickness rated for more than the load, or rig a proper block and tackle with multiple sheaves if more lifting power is needed.
How often should I oil the pivot on my folding pruning knife?

Oil the pivot whenever it begins to feel stiff or gritty, typically every few weeks with regular use. A drop of oil and working the blade open and closed several times keeps movement smooth and prevents rust. Wipe away excess to avoid attracting dirt.
My saw keeps binding and wandering off the line when I cut. Is the wood just too hard?

The saw likely needs sharpening and proper set to the teeth. A dull saw or one with incorrect set will bind and pull to one side regardless of the wood. File each tooth to a sharp point at the proper angle, then set alternate teeth outward slightly so the kerf is wider than the blade.
I want to cut green wood faster. Should I set my saw teeth more aggressively?

Green wood is softer and benefits from larger teeth with more set, which clears the wet sawdust better. However, do not alter a fine-toothed saw meant for dry work; use or acquire a saw designed for rough or green cutting. Proper tooth geometry matters more than force.
I've been using a ladder that has one side rail that feels slightly springy, and I noticed a lengthwise crack in the wood there.

Stop using that ladder immediately, as the cracked rail could fail without warning and cause a dangerous fall. A structural crack in a ladder rail cannot be safely repaired and the ladder must be replaced. Never trust your weight to compromised equipment when a fall could mean serious injury.
How often should I oil the axle of my cart to keep it running smooth?

Oil the axle whenever you hear squeaking or feel resistance in the wheel's turning, and give it a thorough greasing at the start of each heavy-use season. Clean off old buildup and grit before applying fresh tallow or oil, as dirt mixed with grease wears the wood faster. Regular attention prevents costly repairs.
The wooden handle on my splitting maul has cracked near where it meets the head. Can I bind it with wire and keep using it?

A cracked handle will fail without warning and send the head flying, which may cause grave injury. Wire or cord cannot restore the strength that is lost. Fit a new handle properly wedged and seated, or set the tool aside until you can do so.
I need to move a heavy beam. Should I use rope or chain for the pulley rig?

Chain is stronger for its thickness and will not stretch or slip on the sheave, but rope is easier to handle and knot and will show wear before it fails. For heavy loads, use rope of ample thickness—worn or thin rope may part suddenly. Inspect whichever you choose before every use.
My drawknife blade keeps catching and tearing the wood instead of peeling smooth shavings.

The blade has likely dulled or developed nicks along its edge. Resharpen it on a fine stone, working each bevel carefully until you restore a clean edge. A drawknife needs frequent touch-ups when working green wood, so keep a whetstone nearby.
I need to cut a beam overhead but my saw keeps binding and sticking partway through the cut.

The weight of the beam is closing the cut behind your blade as you work. Drive a thin wooden wedge into the cut behind the saw to hold it open, and if possible support both sides of the beam so neither section sags and pinches. Cut from both sides if you can reach them, meeting in the middle.
One wheel on my cart wobbles badly. Can I pack something around the axle to steady it?

The wobble indicates a worn axle hole in the wheel hub or a tapered axle that needs repair. Packing will not solve the problem and the wheel may come off under load. Take the cart to someone who can fit a proper bushing or turn down and re-fit the axle correctly.
The rope on my well bucket is starting to fray near where it rubs the pulley. Can I just keep using it?

A frayed rope under load can snap without warning and cause injury or loss of the bucket. Replace the entire rope now, or at minimum cut away the damaged section and re-splice if enough length remains. Never trust a weakened line for lifting.
My knife blade has a chip in the edge. Can I sharpen it out?

Yes, but you must grind the entire edge back past the deepest point of the chip until the edge is straight again. This takes patience on a coarse stone and will shorten your blade somewhat. Work evenly on both sides to keep the blade symmetrical, then sharpen as usual.
My crosscut saw keeps binding and wandering off the line when I'm cutting thick oak planks. What am I doing wrong?

Check that your saw teeth are evenly set—alternating left and right—to cut a kerf wider than the blade thickness. If the set is uneven or the teeth have lost their sharpness, the blade will bind and follow the grain instead of your line. Resharpen and reset the teeth, and use steady, even strokes without forcing the blade.
My axe head keeps working loose from the handle when I'm splitting logs. I've tried wedging it tighter but it still comes loose after a few swings.

The wood of the handle has likely dried and shrunk since it was fitted. Soak the head in water overnight to swell the wood temporarily, then drive in a new hardwood wedge across the grain of the handle. For a permanent fix, you may need to shape and fit an entirely new handle.
The ladder I'm using has one rung that flexes more than the others when I step on it. Should I avoid that rung?

A rung that flexes differently is cracked, loose in its sockets, or made of weak wood, and it may break without further warning. Do not use that ladder until the defective rung is replaced with sound wood properly fitted and secured. Your weight on a high rung multiplies the force—what feels like slight flex is actually serious weakness.
My ladder has a cracked rung about halfway up. Can I bind it with wire and keep using it, or must I replace the rung?

A cracked rung will fail without warning, and wire binding only conceals the danger. Remove the damaged rung completely and fashion a replacement from sound hardwood, fitting it tightly into the side rails with the grain running lengthwise. Until the repair is made, do not use the ladder at all—a fall from height can cripple or kill.
Can I sharpen my saw by filing the teeth while it is still attached to the frame?

You can, but it is much harder to do properly. The saw should be held rigidly in a vise or clamp at a comfortable working height, which is difficult when the frame is attached. Remove the blade, secure it properly, and file each tooth at the correct angle with steady, even strokes for best results.
My chisel edge is chipped. Can I just grind past the damage on my regular benchstone?

A benchstone removes metal too slowly for repairing chips—you need a coarse grindstone to reshape the edge efficiently, then finish with your benchstone. Take care not to overheat the steel during grinding or you will ruin the temper.
How do I keep my scythe blade from rusting between harvests?

After the season's work, clean the blade thoroughly and coat it with tallow, lard, or a light oil. Store it hanging in a dry place where air can reach all surfaces, never lying on damp earth or stone.
The wheel on my cart wobbles badly but still turns. How urgent is this to fix?

A wobbling wheel will only worsen with use and may fail completely, potentially causing the cart to overturn or breaking the axle. Check whether the hub, spokes, or axle fitting is loose, and make repairs before using the cart with any load. What seems a small problem now can become a dangerous failure on the road.
The wheel on my cart keeps slipping off the axle. If I wedge a bit of rag in there, will that hold?

A rag will compress and fail, letting the wheel come off while the cart is loaded or moving. The axle, hub, or linchpin is worn or damaged—repair or replace the faulty part properly to prevent a dangerous failure.
My pruning saw cuts crooked and binds in green wood even though I just sharpened it. What am I doing wrong?

The teeth likely need proper setting as well as sharpening—they must be bent alternately left and right to cut a kerf wider than the blade thickness. Use a saw set tool to bend each tooth uniformly, then file the teeth to the same height and angle. A saw that cuts crooked may also have uneven set on one side, so check that each tooth is bent the same amount as its partners.
My saw blade wanders off the line when I push hard. What am I doing wrong?

You are likely forcing the cut instead of letting the teeth do the work. Keep the saw sharp, use long steady strokes with light pressure, and ensure your kerf is not binding the blade. A wandering saw often signals dull teeth or improper set.
My cart wheel has developed a slight wobble. Should I grease it or is something else wrong?

A wobble usually means the wheel is loose on the axle or the rim is coming apart from the spokes, not a lubrication problem. Check that the linchpin is secure and the axle fit is tight, then examine the entire wheel for cracked spokes or separating joints. Greasing will not fix structural problems and the wobble will only worsen with use.
My lamp wick keeps smoking and leaving soot everywhere. How do I fix this?

Trim the wick evenly and not too high—a flame drawn too tall burns incompletely and produces smoke. Keep the lamp glass clean and ensure the fuel is good quality, as poor oil also causes sooting. A proper flame burns steady and clear.
The rope on my well bucket is starting to fray near where it rubs the pulley. Should I just turn it around?

Reversing may buy a short time, but a fraying rope under load is a serious hazard. Inspect the entire length carefully—if damage is only at one point and the rest is sound, you may splice in a fresh section, but replacement is safest. A failed rope can cause injury or loss of the bucket, so do not delay the repair.
My plane iron chatters and leaves ridges. I've sharpened it twice but the problem continues. What's wrong?

Chatter usually means the iron isn't seated firmly in the body or the chipbreaker is loose. Check that the wedge or lever cap applies strong, even pressure, ensure the chipbreaker sits tight against the iron with no gap, and verify the frog supports the iron close to the cutting edge.
My chisel keeps slipping off the wood when I try to pare thin shavings. How can I get better control?

A truly sharp chisel will bite into the wood at the lightest touch and let you guide it precisely. Sharpen your blade properly on a fine stone until it will shave hair from your arm. Also check that you're holding the work steady and cutting with the grain rather than against it.
My axe head is loose on the handle and wobbles when I swing it. Can I just tap the wedge in deeper?

If tapping the wedge does not tighten the head securely, the handle has likely shrunk or the eye has worn oversized. Soak the head in water overnight to swell the wood, then drive the wedge firmly; if it still wobbles, you must fit a new handle. A loose axe head is extremely dangerous and can fly off during a swing.
My knife edge has a little chip in it. Can I just sharpen around it?

You must grind the entire edge back past the chip to restore a continuous cutting surface, as the damaged spot will catch and tear rather than cut cleanly. This means removing metal along the whole edge until the chip disappears and you have a smooth bevel again. If the chip is so deep that grinding it out would reduce the blade too much, consider whether the knife is still worth keeping.
One of the wheels on our cart has developed a wobble, and I can see a gap opening between the iron tire and the wooden felloe in places.

The wood has dried and shrunk, loosening the tire, and continued use will quickly destroy the wheel. Take the wheel to someone with equipment to heat and re-set the tire properly while the wood is swollen, or replace the affected sections of felloe if they have cracked. A loose tire will ruin the wheel beyond repair if left unattended.
I'm sharpening a drawknife on my grindstone, but the curved blade is hard to keep at a consistent angle.

Work in sections, sharpening a few inches of the curve at a time while keeping that portion flat against the stone. Rotate the blade gradually as you move along its length, maintaining the bevel angle by feel and frequently checking with your thumb. A rocking motion will round over the bevel and ruin the edge, so patience and small movements serve you better than haste.
My lamp wick burns unevenly and produces black smoke. What causes this?

Trim the wick to an even edge and keep it at the proper height — too high creates smoke and wasted fuel, too low gives poor light. Also ensure your lamp oil is clean; water or sediment in the fuel will cause sputtering and smoking.
My handsaw binds and wanders when cutting thick oak planks. What am I doing wrong?

Check that your saw teeth are properly set — alternate teeth must bend slightly outward to cut a kerf wider than the blade thickness. If the set is correct, the blade itself may have warped from uneven tension; sight down its length to check for twist, and if bent, carefully straighten it or have it trued by someone with experience.
The wooden wheel on my cart has a crack running along the grain. Can I fill it with tar?

Tar or filling will not restore structural strength to a cracked wheel spoke or rim, and the crack will spread further under the cart's weight. The wheel needs proper repair with glued reinforcement, a replacement spoke, or complete replacement depending on the crack's location and severity. A failed wheel can overturn the cart and cause injury or damage.
The leather strop I use for my razor has become hard and shiny. Can this be fixed?

A hard glazed strop will not draw the edge properly and may even dull it. Work neat's-foot oil or tallow into the leather thoroughly and let it absorb overnight, then apply a thin layer of fine abrasive compound. If the surface remains slick and glassy despite treatment, the leather has lost its draw and the strop should be replaced or re-surfaced.
My draw-knife blade keeps chattering and tearing the grain when I work green oak. The edge is sharp enough to shave with.

A shaving-sharp edge on a draw-knife is too thin for green hardwood and will chatter or dig. Hone it to a slightly stouter angle, perhaps thirty degrees, and take lighter cuts with steady even pressure. The edge should bite cleanly without flexing.
My lamp wick keeps smoking no matter how I trim it. What's the fix?

A smoky flame usually means the wick is drawing up impurities from old or poor oil, or the wick itself is clogged with carbon. Clean the lamp thoroughly, refill with fresh clean oil, and trim the wick to an even edge; if it still smokes badly, replace the wick entirely. Breathing lamp smoke day after day is unhealthy and coats everything with soot.
I'm sharpening my axe but one side of the edge is taking longer to form than the other. What am I doing wrong?

You're applying uneven pressure or holding the axe at an inconsistent angle as you work across the stone. Focus on matching your stroke pressure on both sides and maintaining the same bevel throughout. Check your progress frequently by sighting along the edge to see which areas still need work.
My plane blade chatters and leaves ridges instead of smooth shavings. The edge is sharp, so what is wrong?

Chatter usually means the blade is set too deep, too loosely held, or the plane iron cap is not seated tightly behind the edge. Adjust the blade to take a finer cut, ensure the cap iron is tight and close to the edge, and check that the wedge holds everything firm. A properly set plane with a sharp blade should produce thin, continuous shavings and a smooth surface.
I'm cutting green wood and my saw keeps binding in the kerf even though I'm going slow and steady.

Green wood pinches as internal stresses release during cutting. Wedge a small wooden shim into the kerf behind the blade to hold it open, moving it forward as you progress. For deeper cuts, use two wedges and keep them snug against the closing wood.
What's the proper way to sharpen a drawknife that's gone dull from heavy bark stripping?

Clamp the drawknife securely and use a smooth file or sharpening stone on the beveled side only, maintaining the original angle of the edge. Work along the entire length evenly, then remove any burr from the flat back side with a few light strokes. Test the edge on a wood scrap—it should pare thin shavings cleanly without tearing the grain.
The oil lamp chimney is blackened with soot. Should I scrape it clean?

Wash the chimney in warm soapy water rather than scraping, which can scratch the glass. The soot indicates the wick is too high or needs trimming; lower it and trim the charred top evenly so the flame burns clean and steady without smoking.
My lamp wick keeps burning unevenly and smoking. What causes this?

The wick is likely trimmed unevenly or has become clogged with carbon deposits. Trim it straight across to an even height when the lamp is cool, and clean off any blackened crust. Also check that the wick is properly centered in the burner and that you are not turning the flame up too high for the amount of air reaching it.
The wooden mallet I use for chisels has split at the striking end. Can I keep using it carefully?

The split will worsen with each blow and pieces may fly off, potentially striking your eyes or hands. Make or obtain a new mallet head; the work is simple and the risk is not worth taking. A sound mallet is essential for controlled chisel work, and a damaged one compromises both safety and precision.
The wooden bed of my plane has a long crack running with the grain. Will soaking it in oil keep it from splitting further?

Oil may slow moisture changes but will not repair a structural crack—the bed must bear considerable pressure and a split compromises accuracy and safety. Replace the body or have a new one made; a failed plane can ruin workpieces and injure your hands.
The rope on my well pulley has started to fray near where it runs over the wheel. Can I just rotate it so the worn part is elsewhere?

Moving the worn section only delays the inevitable and risks sudden failure when the rope is loaded. Replace the entire rope before it breaks, as a falling bucket can injure anyone below or damage the well lining. Inspect the pulley wheel for rough spots or cracks that may have caused the fraying.
When I'm splitting logs, should I aim for the center or look for natural cracks?

Look for existing cracks, checks, or the natural divisions between growth rings and aim your wedge or axe there. Wood splits far more easily along the grain and existing weaknesses than through solid cross-section. Starting at the edge and working inward also works better than striking dead center.
Can I sharpen my knife on the same stone I use for axes and other heavy tools?

You can, but use a finer-grit portion of the stone or a separate finishing stone for the knife to achieve the keener edge it needs. Coarse stones suited to axes leave scratches that weaken a thin blade. Keep different areas of your stone dressed for different purposes.
What is the right way to store my chisels so they stay sharp longer?

Keep them in a rack or wrapped individually so the edges never touch each other or hard surfaces. Store them in a dry place, and consider a light coating of oil on the metal if they will sit unused for some time. Even light contact with other tools or jostling in a box will dull and chip the cutting edges.
I found my grandfather's old chisel rusted in the shed. How can I bring it back to working condition?

Remove the rust with a fine stone and oil, working patiently to reveal clean metal beneath. Check carefully for any pitting or cracks that would weaken the blade. Once cleaned, sharpen it properly on your grindstone and keep it oiled to prevent future rust.
I need to splice a rope that's too short for the job. What's the safest way to join two pieces for lifting loads?
