A short splice is strongest for joining rope, though it thickens the line where joined. Unlay several inches of each end, marry the strands together, and tuck each strand over-and-under through the standing part at least three times. Never trust a knot alone for heavy loads.
When sharpening my scythe with the whetstone, should I push into the edge or draw away from it?

Draw the stone along the blade from heel to point while moving away from the edge, maintaining the existing bevel angle. Pushing into the edge risks catching and rolling the delicate cutting surface. Keep the stone wet and work both sides evenly to preserve the blade's balance.
I'm trying to hang a heavy pulley block from a beam. How do I know if the beam will hold the load safely?

Examine the beam carefully for cracks, rot, insect damage, or previous splitting, especially near knots or where you plan to attach the hardware. A sound beam of adequate size will hold considerable weight, but any structural weakness can lead to sudden failure under load. If you have any doubt about the beam's integrity, reinforce it or choose a stronger location.
My saw cuts crooked no matter how carefully I guide it. What am I doing wrong?

The teeth are likely uneven or the set is wrong on one side, causing the blade to pull. Check that the teeth are uniform in height and equally bent outward on alternating sides. If the saw is properly sharpened and set but still wanders, focus on starting the cut square and letting the saw do the work without forcing it.
The edge of my splitting maul has mushroomed and bits of metal flake off when I strike. Can I keep using it?

A mushroomed striking edge throws dangerous metal fragments that can injure your eyes or hands. Grind back the damaged metal on a stone until you have clean edges again, working carefully to preserve the basic shape, then dress any burrs before returning the tool to service.
I'm cutting timber with a crosscut saw and the kerf keeps binding no matter how carefully I work. What am I doing wrong?

Your saw likely needs setting—the teeth must be bent slightly outward to cut a kerf wider than the blade. Without proper set, the blade pinches in its own cut. Take the saw to someone with a setting tool, or learn the technique yourself; it makes all the difference between misery and clean work.
The ladder I'm using has a cracked rung about halfway up. Can I just avoid stepping on that one?

Do not use a ladder with any cracked or damaged rungs, as the structure is compromised and other rungs may fail under load. Replace the broken rung with sound wood of the same species and dimensions, properly mortised and secured, before climbing again.
The wick on my lamp keeps smoking and the flame is dim even when I trim it. What could be wrong?

The wick may be clogged with carbon buildup or the fuel may be contaminated or of poor quality. Trim away all charred portions of the wick and ensure your fuel is clean and appropriate for the lamp. If smoking continues, the chimney may need cleaning or the wick may require replacement.
The rope on my well pulley is fraying near the bucket knot. Can I just tie it higher up?

Frayed rope is weakened and may break under load, dropping the bucket or worse. Inspect the entire length for damage, and if any section is worn, replace the whole rope. A failed rope can cause injury or loss of your bucket.
The wooden handle on my hammer has a crack running lengthwise near where it meets the head.

That crack will widen under striking and the head may fly off, causing serious injury. Replace the handle entirely rather than trying to bind or glue the split wood. A failed handle during a swing has broken bones and worse.
The wooden handle on my hammer has a crack running lengthwise about halfway up from where it meets the head.

Replace the handle immediately before it fails and the head flies free, which could cause serious injury. A cracked handle cannot be reliably repaired and will only worsen under the shock of striking. Fit a new handle of sound, straight-grained hardwood, properly wedged and seated.
The grindstone wobbles slightly as it spins. Does this matter for sharpening?

Yes, wobble produces an uneven bevel and makes the tool difficult to control safely against the stone. The axle may be bent or the stone poorly mounted; inspect and correct the cause before continuing. A true-running stone is essential for both quality and safety.
I dropped my best chisel and now there's a small chip in the cutting edge. Can I work around it?

A chipped edge will catch and tear wood fibers rather than cutting cleanly, ruining your work. Grind the edge back past the chip on the stone until you reach sound metal, then re-establish the bevel — it's a small loss in length but restores proper function.
One spoke on my cart wheel has split along the grain about halfway up. Can I wrap it with wet rawhide to strengthen it?

A split spoke weakens the entire wheel and will worsen under the cart's weight, especially on uneven ground. Remove and replace the damaged spoke with sound wood, properly fitted and driven tight. Binding may hold for a short while, but the spoke will eventually fail and could cause the wheel to collapse when loaded.
I want to split this log but it's knotted all through. Should I just hit it harder with the axe?

Knotted wood resists the axe and may cause the blade to glance or stick dangerously. Use iron wedges driven with a maul instead, working from multiple points around the knots. If it still refuses to split cleanly, set it aside for a use that doesn't require splitting—some wood is better left whole.
The wooden handle on my hammer is loose in the head. Can I just nail it tight?

Never nail a hammer handle—it will split the wood and fail under use. Drive a wooden wedge into the kerf at the top of the handle to expand it firmly within the eye. If the handle is worn smooth or cracked, replace it entirely before the head flies loose during a swing.
I've been using my ladder on soft ground and now one leg has sunk deeper than the other. Is this safe?

No, a ladder on uneven footing is dangerous and may slip or tip when you shift your weight. Set both feet on firm, level ground, or place a wide board beneath both legs to distribute the load evenly. Never climb a ladder that rocks or leans to one side.
My plane blade chatters and leaves ridges instead of smooth cuts. What am I doing wrong?

The blade is likely dull, set too deep, or not seated firmly in the plane body. Sharpen the iron to a keen edge, ensure the cap iron sits tight against it with no gap, and adjust for a finer cut. Press down firmly on the fore of the plane at the start of each stroke and on the rear at the finish.
The leather strop I use after sharpening has gotten hard and smooth. Does it still work the same?

A hard, glazed strop has lost its ability to polish the edge properly. Roughen the surface slightly with fine sand or powdered stone, then work in tallow or neat's-foot oil to restore the leather's slight draw and grip.
The wheel on my cart has started making a terrible squealing sound and feels hot to the touch after I've been driving it a while.

The axle is running dry and the friction is creating heat that can char the wood or even start a fire. Remove the wheel, clean the axle thoroughly, and apply a generous coating of grease or tallow to the bearing surfaces. Check that the wheel isn't fitted too tightly, as it needs slight play to turn freely.
The wood handle on my hammer has a long crack running from where the head sits down toward the grip. It hasn't broken yet though.

That crack will grow with each strike until the handle fails, and the head may fly off with considerable force in any direction. Replace the handle immediately—a cracked hammer handle is among the most dangerous tool faults, as you cannot predict when or how it will break.
I need to sharpen my scythe blade but I'm not sure what angle to hold the stone at or how to keep it even along the whole curve.

Sit with the scythe across your lap, edge facing away, and work the stone along the blade from tang to point in smooth sweeping strokes. Keep the stone tilted to match the existing bevel—usually quite shallow—and make several passes on one side before turning to remove the burr from the other. The rhythm comes with practice; listen for the even sound of the stone against metal.
I'm cutting mortises in white pine for a door frame. The chisel keeps following the grain and wandering off the line.

Soft woods require shallow cuts and frequent realignment. Score your mortise boundaries deeply with a marking knife, and pare no more than a quarter-inch depth at a time, keeping the flat back of the chisel against the scored line. Work from both ends toward the middle.
The rope on my well pulley has gotten stiff and some of the strands are broken. Can I still use it if I'm careful?

No, replace it immediately. A rope supporting weight overhead must be completely sound, as broken strands indicate the whole line is deteriorating and may fail without warning. The cost of new rope is nothing compared to the danger of a bucket or load falling on someone below.
My plane blade chatters and leaves ripples in the wood surface. What causes this?

Chatter usually comes from a blade that is not seated firmly, has too much projection, or lacks a sharp edge. Tighten the wedge or cap iron, reduce the blade depth slightly, and ensure the edge is freshly honed. The plane should glide smoothly and leave a clean surface.
Can I sharpen my saw myself or should I take it to someone?

If you have a saw file, steady hands, and patience to learn, you can maintain your own saws. Each tooth must be filed to the same height, angle, and set. However, if the teeth are badly damaged or uneven, or if you lack confidence, a skilled sawyer will restore it properly for a modest fee.
Can I use my carpenter's hatchet to split kindling if I'm careful?

A hatchet may split small kindling, but repeated splitting will damage the thin edge meant for trimming. Use a proper splitting maul or the poll of a felling axe for this work, reserving the hatchet for cutting and shaping. The right tool for each task prevents breakage and keeps edges keen.
My handsaw cuts crooked no matter how carefully I follow the line.

The saw teeth are likely set unevenly, causing the blade to pull to one side. Check the set with your eye down the length of the blade, and use a saw-set tool to adjust the teeth so they bend equally on both sides. If the blade itself is kinked or bent, it may need professional straightening or replacement.
The grindstone wobbles on its axle and grinds unevenly. What's the remedy?

Check that the axle runs true and is properly seated in its bearings. If the stone itself is worn unevenly, dress it back to round with a stone pick or devil, working carefully to restore a true surface for even grinding.
The grinding wheel wobbles badly and makes my chisels uneven. Can I fix this myself?

A wobbling wheel is usually poorly mounted or cracked, and continuing to use it risks shattering the stone. Check that the axle fits snugly and the wheel sits square on its mounting; if the stone itself is damaged or worn unevenly, replace it. A true wheel is essential for proper sharpening.
The iron wedge on my felling axe has slipped down and the handle feels loose in my hand when I swing. What should I do?

Stop using it immediately, as a loose head is deadly. Drive the wedge deeper into the handle kerf, and if that fails to tighten it properly, fit a new handle — your life depends on the head staying fast.
How often should I oil the pivot points on my post drill to keep it working smoothly?

Oil all pivot points and the rack-and-pinion mechanism monthly if you use the drill regularly, or before each use if it sits idle for long periods. Wipe away old oil and grit first, then apply a light machine oil or rendered fat, working the handle through its full range to distribute the lubricant evenly.
I'm having trouble keeping my plane iron at a steady angle while sharpening. Any tricks to help?

Hold the iron so your fingers rest against the stone's surface, using them as a guide to maintain the angle, and make long steady strokes using your whole arm rather than just your wrist. Some craftsmen fix a wooden block to the back of the iron at the desired angle to serve as a guide. Practice on a worn-out iron until the motion becomes steady before sharpening your good tools.
The rope on my pulley is starting to fray near the hook. How much longer will it last?

Frayed rope is approaching failure and cannot be trusted with loads. Replace it now—rope is far cheaper than the injury or damage from a sudden break. Inspect all rope regularly and retire any showing worn fibers, especially near stress points like knots and hardware.
The ladder rungs feel a bit loose when I climb. Should I worry?

Yes, loose rungs are dangerous and can give way under your weight. Drive wooden wedges into the joints from the side if there is room, or drill and peg them securely. If the wood is rotted or split at the joints, that ladder is unsafe and you must repair it properly or build a new one.
How often should I oil the wheel bearings on my handcart?

Oil the bearings whenever you notice the wheel turning less freely or hear any grinding sound, and always after the cart has been exposed to heavy rain or wet conditions. Regular light oiling prevents the damage that comes from metal wearing against dry metal.
My axe head keeps working loose from the handle when I'm splitting wood. Should I just drive it back on tighter each time?

A loose head is dangerous and will only worsen with repeated striking. Remove the head, check if the handle eye is split or worn thin at the top, and replace the handle if damaged. If sound, reseat it firmly, then drive a wooden wedge across the grain at the top to spread the wood and lock it tight.
My gouge keeps catching and digging into the wood instead of cutting smoothly. Is the edge too sharp?

The problem is likely a wrong cutting angle or a burr remaining on the inside edge, not excessive sharpness. Keep the bevel in contact with the wood and the handle raised so the tool rides on its bevel without the edge digging in. Check the inside of the gouge for any burr and remove it carefully with a slipstone shaped to the curve.
I'm sharpening my chisel on the grindstone but one side of the edge is wearing down faster than the other. Why does this keep happening?

You're applying uneven pressure or holding the chisel at a slight angle to the stone's face. Keep both hands balanced and press the blade flat against the stone, moving it steadily across the full width. Check your stone as well—if it's worn unevenly, dress it flat with a harder stone or coarse sand before continuing.
One wheel on my cart is starting to come loose from the hub. Can I just drive the spokes in tighter with a mallet?

The wood has likely dried and shrunk, and hammering may crack the spokes or hub. Soaking the wheel in water will cause the wood to swell and tighten the joints temporarily, but a wheelwright should properly assess whether the wheel needs re-setting or replacement. A wheel that fails under load can cause serious injury.
The stove door doesn't close tightly anymore and smoke leaks out around the edges. How can I seal it better?

The door or frame has likely warped from repeated heating, or the latch has worn and no longer pulls tight. Check if the hinges are loose or bent first, as these can prevent proper seating. If the metal itself has warped significantly, you'll need a blacksmith to straighten it or fit a new door—stuffing gaps with cloth or clay creates fire danger.
The wheel on my cart is making a grinding noise. Should I grease the axle more heavily?

Grinding usually means grit has gotten into the hub or the bearing surfaces are worn. Remove the wheel, clean out all old grease and dirt thoroughly, then inspect the axle and hub for scoring or uneven wear. If the surfaces are damaged, they must be repaired or replaced; simply adding grease will only quicken the destruction.
The grindstone wobbles badly on its axle. Can I pack something around the axle hole to steady it?

Packing the hole risks the stone shattering when spinning under pressure. Check if the axle itself is bent or worn unevenly, and straighten or replace it if so. If the stone's center hole has worn oval, the stone must be retired from use, as no repair will make it safe.
My ladder feels steady enough but one rung has a knot in the wood right in the middle. Should I worry about it?

A knot in the center of a rung is a serious weakness that may give way under your weight, especially as the wood ages and dries. Replace that rung with a piece of straight-grained wood free of knots. Your life depends on every rung holding firm when you are above the ground.
The handle on my felling axe has a crack running halfway through. Can I wrap it with wire to keep using it?

No—replace the handle immediately. Wire wrapping will not restore strength, and the handle will fail suddenly under the shock of a hard swing, putting you and anyone nearby at serious risk. A cracked axe handle is among the most dangerous tool faults to ignore.
How often should I oil the moving parts on my pulleys and block tackle?

Oil the sheave pins and any metal bearings whenever they begin to feel stiff or make noise, typically every few weeks with regular use. Wipe away old oil and dirt first, apply fresh oil sparingly, and work the parts to distribute it. Too much oil collects dust and grit, causing more wear than it prevents.
My chisel edge went dull very quickly even though I just sharpened it. Could I have done something wrong at the stone?

A keen edge that dulls swiftly was likely sharpened at too shallow an angle, leaving fragile metal that crumbles in use. Grind a proper bevel—around thirty degrees for general work—then hone it smooth. Also ensure you're not striking the chisel into hidden nails or working wood with embedded grit.
There's surface rust on my saw blade from being stored damp. Will it hurt the cutting or just look poor?

Surface rust creates friction that makes the saw bind and drag through the cut, wearing you out needlessly. Clean it thoroughly with fine abrasive and oil, then keep the blade lightly oiled when stored. Rust also provides footing for deeper pitting if left unchecked, which will eventually ruin the set of the teeth.
My wood plane blade chatters and leaves ridges instead of smooth shavings, even after I sharpened it. What needs fixing?

The blade is likely not seated firmly against the frog or the chipbreaker is set too far back from the cutting edge. Disassemble the plane, clean all mating surfaces, and reassemble with the chipbreaker very close to the edge—no more than the thickness of a shaving. Ensure the blade sits flat with no rocking and the wedge or lever cap applies even pressure across the full width.
I left my good plane on the workbench and now there's a patch of rust on the sole from some water that dripped on it overnight.

Rub the rust off with fine sand or emery powder and oil, working along the length of the sole. Once clean, oil the entire surface and wipe away the excess. In the future, always stand your plane on its side rather than its sole, and keep a light coat of oil on all metal parts.
I sharpened my chisel but now it has a burr along the edge. How do I fix this?

Lay the flat back of the chisel against your finest stone and draw it back a few times to remove the burr. Then make one or two light passes with the bevel side to finish the edge. The burr forms naturally during sharpening but must be removed for a clean cut.
My shovel handle cracked near the socket. Can I bind it with wire and keep using it?

A cracked handle will fail under load and may injure you when it breaks. Replace the handle entirely; the socket can be reused with a properly fitted new shaft. Binding a structural crack with wire creates false confidence in a weakened tool.
The whetstone I use for my scythe has a hollow worn into the middle from years of sharpening. Does this matter?

That hollow will prevent you from maintaining a consistent bevel and will eventually round over the edge instead of sharpening it properly. You need to dress the stone flat again using coarse sand and water on a flat surface, or replace it if it's worn too thin to be worth the labor.
My lamp wick keeps smoking and the glass is blackening. What's causing this?

A smoking wick is burning too rich, either because it's turned up too high or the wick is of poor quality or badly trimmed. Lower the flame until the smoke stops, trim the wick evenly across the top, and keep the glass clean. If it continues smoking at a low flame, the wick may need replacement.
The stove door doesn't seat properly and smoke leaks out. Can I pack the gap with ash to seal it temporarily?

Ash will not seal reliably and may worsen the draft problem. Check if the door is warped or if the frame has shifted, then adjust the hinges or straighten the frame as needed. If the door itself is damaged beyond adjustment, have it repaired or replaced to prevent dangerous smoke in the room.
How do I stop my rope from unraveling at the cut end?

Whip the end tightly with thin twine, wrapping a finger's length of the rope to bind all strands together. Alternatively, if working near a flame, you may carefully singe natural fiber rope ends to fuse them, though whipping is more reliable for heavy use.
The wooden handle on my hammer has a crack running lengthwise near where it meets the head. Can I bind it with wire to keep using it?

A cracked handle near the head is dangerous and will fail when you need the tool most, likely sending the head flying. Replace the handle entirely with sound wood, fitted and wedged properly. No amount of binding will restore the strength needed where the greatest force is applied.
My grindstone seems to cut slower than it used to, even after I dress the surface. What gives?

The stone may be glazed with metal particles filling the pores, which you can remedy by dressing more aggressively with a star-wheel dresser or a piece of soft brick. Check also that the stone runs true without wobble and that you're applying steady light pressure with plenty of water. A stone that has become too smooth from fine work may need roughening for faster cutting.
The wooden handle on my splitting maul has a crack running about two inches down from where it meets the head. Is it safe to keep using?

That crack will only grow worse under the shock of splitting, and the head may fly loose and cause grave injury. Replace the handle entirely before using the maul again, fitting it tight with proper wedges.
I want to sharpen my scythe but I've only ever seen it done, never done it myself. What's the most important thing to get right?

Keep the whetstone moving along the entire edge at a consistent shallow angle, following the existing bevel rather than inventing a new one. Work both sides evenly with smooth strokes, and test sharpness on a grass stem rather than your thumb.
The ladder rungs creak loudly when I climb. Is this normal wear?

Creaking often indicates loose joints or cracking wood, both of which compromise safety. Inspect each rung carefully for splits, check that mortises are tight, and do not use the ladder for overhead work until repairs are made. A fall from height can be fatal.
The wick in my lamp has gotten crusted and burned down short. Can I just trim off the bad part and keep using it?

A crusted wick draws poorly and smokes terribly, wasting oil and fouling your room with soot. Pull it out, trim away all the burned portion until you reach clean fiber, or replace it entirely if too short. A proper wick gives steady light without waste or trouble.
The handle on my axe is loose and wobbles when I swing it. Can I just wrap rope around it to tighten it up?

A loose axe head is extremely dangerous and rope will not secure it properly. Drive a hardwood wedge into the end of the handle through the eye of the head, and if there is room, add a cross wedge of metal. If the handle is split or too worn to hold wedges, replace it entirely before use.
My axe handle has a long crack running with the grain. Can I bind it with wire?

No, replace the handle entirely. A cracked handle can split completely during a swing, sending the axe head flying or causing you to lose control. Wire binding may hold for light use but creates false confidence in a fundamentally unsafe tool.
I need to move a heavy millstone across my yard. What's the safest way?

Build a low wooden frame that cradles the stone, then use a lever and fulcrum to tip it onto its edge so it can roll. Guide it slowly with ropes on either side, keeping hands and feet clear of the path. Never try to carry such weight directly, and ensure your path is level and free of obstructions.
I'm cutting timber with a two-man crosscut saw and my partner says I'm pushing instead of just pulling on my stroke. How do I fix that?

The saw cuts only on the pull; pushing bows the blade and binds it in the kerf. Let the saw glide forward without force when your partner pulls, then draw it smoothly back toward yourself with steady pressure. Trust the teeth to do their work—your task is rhythm and direction, not force.
The wheel on my cart wobbles badly. Can I just tighten the linchpin or do I need to fix something else?

Check whether the axle is worn, the hub is loose on the axle, or the spokes have loosened in the hub. Tightening the linchpin only keeps the wheel from falling off, it does not fix wobble. Tap loose spokes tight, repair or replace a worn hub, and ensure the axle is straight and properly fitted.
My handsaw binds and wanders when cutting thick oak planks. What am I doing wrong?

The teeth likely need sharpening and proper set—each tooth bent slightly outward in alternating directions so the kerf is wider than the blade. Keep your strokes long and steady, letting the saw's weight do the work rather than forcing it. If the blade still wanders, check that you're sawing square to the face and that the teeth have uniform height.
I want to splice two ropes together to get more length for lifting. What's a splice that won't come apart under load?

A proper long splice maintains nearly the full strength of the rope by interweaving the strands over a foot or more of length. Unlay several inches of each rope end, marry them together, then tuck each strand over and under through the standing part following the original lay. A short splice is stronger still but creates a thick spot that will not pass through a pulley.
The wooden handle on my hammer has split near where it enters the head. Can this be fixed?

A split handle is dangerous and cannot be reliably repaired — the shock of striking will worsen the crack and the head may fly loose. Replace the handle entirely with sound hardwood, ensuring the grain runs parallel to the length and the wedges are driven tight.
My chisel edge went dull after hitting a nail hidden in old timber. How do I get it sharp again?

You must first grind away the rolled or chipped edge on a coarse stone until you reach sound metal and restore the proper bevel angle. Then work through finer stones to bring back a keen edge, keeping the angle steady throughout.
I'm cutting a mortise with my chisel and the edges keep crumbling instead of cutting clean. What am I doing wrong?

Your chisel is likely dull or you are trying to remove too much wood at once. Sharpen the chisel properly on a stone until it can shave wood cleanly, and work in thin layers, especially near the edges of the mortise. Keep the bevel facing into the waste wood and strike squarely; rushing or prying will tear the grain and ruin the joint.
I'm sharpening my chisel on the grindstone and the edge is turning blue from the heat. Should I keep going?

Stop immediately and let the blade cool — the blue color shows you have overheated the steel and destroyed its temper. Grind slowly with frequent water cooling, and grind away the discolored metal before resharpening carefully. A burned edge will not hold sharpness no matter how keenly you hone it.
My ladder feels unsteady when I climb it even though the rails aren't cracked. What should I check?

Examine the rungs where they enter the rails; they may have loosened in their sockets even if no crack is visible. Test each one by hand for movement, and also sight down the rails to see if the ladder has twisted out of true. A twisted or loose-rung ladder cannot be trusted with your weight.
My grindstone wobbles badly and makes uneven contact with the tool. Should I just press harder on the low spots?

Pressing harder will only worsen the uneven wear and risks damaging your tools. The stone needs truing with a dressing tool or softer stone to restore a flat, even surface. If the wobble comes from a bent shaft or loose mounting, repair the mechanical fault before further use.
My hatchet head keeps working loose from the handle when I split kindling. I've tried wedging it tighter but it loosens again after a few days of work.

The wood handle has likely dried and shrunk since it was first fitted. Soak the head in a bucket of water overnight to swell the wood fibers back into a tight fit, then store the tool in a place with more even moisture when not in use. If soaking no longer helps, the handle must be replaced entirely with a new shaft properly wedged at fitting.
My planing blade chatters and leaves ridges in the wood no matter how I adjust the iron. What should I check?

Check that the blade is seated flat against the frog with no debris underneath, and ensure the wedge or cap iron holds it firmly without any play. The blade itself may have developed a hollow or uneven back from improper sharpening—sight down its length and flatten the back on a stone if needed. A loose frog, cracked bed, or worn adjustment mechanism can also prevent proper seating.
My grindstone has a deep groove worn in it. Does that matter for sharpening?

Yes, the groove will prevent proper contact with the full width of your blade and create uneven bevels. Dress the stone with a pick or star-wheel dresser to restore a flat, even surface. A true grindstone face is essential for accurate edge geometry.
The bottom rung of my ladder cracked right through. Can I bind it with wire and keep using it?

A cracked rung will fail under your weight when you least expect it. Wire binding cannot restore the wood's strength and creates a false sense of security. Replace the rung entirely with sound wood of the same type and dimensions, fitted and fastened as the original.
I'm sharpening my knife on a stone but one side of the edge seems to wear away faster than the other, making it crooked.

You're applying uneven pressure or holding the blade at different angles on each side. Count your strokes and make the same number on each side, keeping your wrist locked at a consistent angle throughout. Check the edge against the light frequently—a crooked edge catches light unevenly and will only worsen if you continue the same pattern.
I need to move a heavy barrel up a ramp into the wagon. What's the safest way without it rolling back on me?

Rig a rope through a pulley anchored above the wagon bed, then tie it securely around the barrel's middle. As you pull from the wagon end, have a second person place wooden chocks behind the barrel after each heave, so it cannot roll backward. Never stand directly downhill of a heavy load on a slope.
My lantern glass is cracked but the flame still burns fine behind it. Is it safe to keep using until I can get a replacement?

No—a cracked glass can shatter from the heat at any moment, exposing the open flame to surroundings and potentially starting a fire. Extinguish it and leave it unlit until the glass is properly replaced. Use another light source in the meantime.
The wooden ladder up to the hayloft has a cracked rail on one side. It still feels sturdy enough. Should I be concerned?

Yes, replace or repair it before using it again. Cracks in ladder rails propagate suddenly under load, and a failure halfway up could cause serious injury. Either sister a reinforcing piece firmly alongside the cracked rail, or build a new ladder if the damage is extensive.
My handsaw keeps binding and wandering off the line when I cut thick oak boards. The teeth look sharp enough to me.

Sharp teeth alone do not make a good saw — the set matters as much. Each tooth must be bent slightly outward, alternating left and right, so the kerf is wider than the blade itself. Check your set with a straightedge and use a saw-set tool to adjust the bend evenly on both sides.
My draw knife keeps digging in too deep and getting stuck. How should I adjust my grip or angle?

Hold the draw knife at a low slicing angle to the wood, almost flat, rather than digging the edge in steeply. Pull with steady even pressure using your whole body, not just your arms, and skew the blade slightly so it slices across the grain. Keep the edge sharp—a dull draw knife requires excessive force and catches rather than paring smoothly.
My axe head keeps working loose from the handle during use. I've tried wedging it tighter but it loosens again after a few swings.

The wood has likely dried and shrunk since fitting. Soak the head end of the handle in water overnight to swell the wood, then drive in a proper hardwood wedge across the grain while still damp. If the eye of the axe head has become worn or enlarged, the handle must be replaced with one properly sized to fit tight.
The grinding wheel wobbles on its axle when I turn it. Is this merely annoying or actually dangerous?

A wobbling grindstone is dangerous and will only worsen. The wobble indicates a loose mounting or damaged bearing that can let the heavy stone shift or come free entirely while spinning. Stop using it immediately, check that the axle and mounting holes are not worn oval, and secure everything properly before grinding again.
Can I store my good steel tools in the barn through winter, or should I bring them inside?

Bring them inside or rust will claim them. Cold itself does no harm, but barns trap moisture from animals and snow that will corrode unprotected metal. A light coat of oil and storage in a dry place preserves your tools for years.
How often should I oil my saw blade to keep it from rusting?

Wipe the blade with an oiled rag after each use, especially if it has gotten damp. A thin coat of oil prevents rust and keeps the blade cutting smoothly. Store saws in a dry place, and check them regularly for any spots of rust to address early.
The wooden handle on my sledge has a crack running halfway down from the head. Can I just wrap it tight with wire and keep working?

A cracked sledge handle will fail without warning, likely when you swing hardest, and send the head flying toward anyone nearby. Replace the handle entirely before using the tool again. No binding or wrapping makes split wood trustworthy under such force.
My splitting maul keeps glancing off hardwood rounds instead of biting in. What am I doing wrong?

A dull or improperly ground edge will bounce rather than split. Take the maul to a grindstone and restore a proper wedge taper—not sharp like an axe, but a clean angle without rounding. Also check that you strike square to the grain and aim for existing cracks when possible.
When I'm splitting wood, sometimes the axe glances off and nearly hits my leg. How can I prevent this?

Always position yourself so that if the axe glances or misses, it travels away from your body and legs. Stand with your feet well apart and to the side of your swing path, and make sure the chopping block is stable and at proper height. If you cannot split safely, stop and reassess your stance and target.
My chisel edge has a few tiny chips in it from hitting a nail hidden in old timber. Do I need to grind past them all?

Yes, grind the edge back until all chips disappear and you reach sound metal throughout, even if this takes considerable material. A chipped edge will never cut cleanly and the damaged spots will spread into larger cracks under pressure. The time spent restoring a proper edge is far less than fighting a faulty tool.
When I'm splitting wood with my maul, the handle sometimes strikes the round instead of just the head. Will this hurt the tool?

Striking the handle against wood will eventually split or weaken it, creating danger when the head comes loose. Improve your aim and follow-through so only the metal contacts the round, and consider whether your handle is too long for controlled swings. If the handle shows any cracks from impacts, replace it before it fails under a heavy strike.
My ladder rungs feel loose when I shake the rails. Is this a serious problem?

Yes, loose rungs can rotate or pull free under your weight, causing falls. Re-glue and peg them securely before any further use, checking each joint is tight. Never trust a ladder with compromised joints for overhead work.
My lamp wick keeps smoking no matter how I trim it. Does it just need more oil in the reservoir?

Black smoke means incomplete burning, usually from a wick turned too high or a chimney starved of air. Lower the flame until it burns clear and yellow, check that air holes are not blocked, and ensure the chimney glass is clean. Oil level does not affect smoke unless so low the wick draws unevenly.
My rope has a few strands broken in one spot about midway along. Is it still good for hoisting loads?

A rope with broken strands has lost strength and will likely fail at that weak point under load, especially with any shock or swing. Retire that rope from hoisting or critical use entirely. You may cut it and use the sound portions for light tasks where a failure would not cause harm.
My chisel edge rolled over when I struck a knot. Should I just grind it back to shape?

Grinding removes metal quickly but generates heat that can ruin the temper if not done carefully. Dip the tool frequently in water to keep it cool, or use a coarse whetstone instead, which is slower but safer. Restore the proper bevel angle and then hone the edge.
The wooden handle on my knife is cracked lengthwise. Can I wrap it with leather to hold it together?

Leather wrapping will not repair a split handle and may hide worsening damage until the knife fails in use. Remove the old handle completely and fit a new one of sound hardwood, properly shaped and secured. A knife with a compromised handle is dangerous, as your grip may slip during cutting.
I want to sharpen my knife to a finer edge. Should I use more pressure on the stone?

More pressure is not the answer and may round the bevel or overheat the edge. Instead, progress from a coarser stone to a finer one, maintaining a consistent angle with light, even strokes. Finish on your finest stone or a leather strop to polish away the last roughness.
The axe head keeps slipping on the handle when I split wood. What should I do?

Stop using it immediately—a loose axe head is deadly. Remove the head, check both handle and eye for damage, then fit a new handle if needed and secure it with proper wedges driven crosswise. Test the fit thoroughly before any further use.
The wheel on my cart is starting to come loose from the axle. Can I just tap it back on and keep using it?

A loose wheel will work itself farther off with every turn and may fly free entirely, wrecking the cart or causing injury. Remove the wheel, examine both the axle end and the hub for wear, and secure it properly with a new pin or wedge. If wear has made the fit sloppy, the parts need repair or replacement.
My wood chisel edge keeps chipping and rolling over even after I sharpen it. The steel seems too soft.

If the edge won't hold even after proper sharpening, the steel has likely lost its temper from overheating during grinding or previous misuse. You can sometimes restore it by careful re-hardening and tempering if you have the skill and equipment, but this requires heating to the right color and quenching properly. Otherwise, the chisel needs replacement or attention from a skilled blacksmith.
I need to splice two lengths of rope together for a longer line. What's the strongest way to join them?

For a lasting splice, unlay several inches of each rope end, trim half the strands from each, then interweave the remaining strands by tucking them over and under the standing strands of the opposite rope. Work it tight as you go and finish by trimming excess. A proper splice keeps nearly the full strength of the rope, unlike a knot which weakens it considerably.
The wooden handle on my sledge has split lengthwise near where the head sits.

That handle is no longer safe to use, as it may fail completely during a swing and cause injury. Replace it entirely with sound ash or hickory, fitted tightly through the head. Never attempt to bind or glue a split striking-tool handle, as the forces involved are too great.
The wick in my lamp is burned down short. Can I pull more up from the holder, or do I need a new one?

If there is clean wick remaining below, you can carefully draw it up; if it is charred throughout or too short to adjust, replace it entirely. A badly burned wick smokes heavily, wastes oil, and gives poor light.
The door on my stove won't stay closed properly and smoke leaks out around the edges when I have a fire going.

The door has likely warped from heat or the hinges have loosened, creating gaps that break the seal. Check that the hinges are tight and properly aligned first. If the door itself is twisted, it may need to be replaced, as a leaking stove wastes fuel and fills the room with smoke. Some gaps can be temporarily packed with stove clay, but a properly fitted door is the real solution.
My cart wheel wobbles because the hub is worn loose on the axle. Can I shim it with wood scraps to tighten it up?

Temporary wooden shims may get you home, but the hub needs proper repair—either bushing the worn hole or fitting a larger axle pin. A wheel that comes off while the cart is loaded can cause injury and destroy the wheel itself. Address the root cause rather than patching the symptom.
I need to fell a leaning tree but it's leaning toward the barn. How should I handle this?

Do not attempt to fell a tree against its natural lean without proper equipment and expertise. Either hire someone experienced with wedges and tackle to control the fall, or limb the side away from the barn to shift the balance before cutting. Misjudging a leaning tree can cause serious damage or death.
How often should I oil the moving parts on my pulley block?

Oil the sheave pins and any metal-on-metal bearing surfaces whenever the pulley begins to feel stiff or makes noise, which might be every few weeks with daily use. Use a light oil or rendered fat, wiping away excess so it does not attract dirt that would create grinding paste.
How often should I clean out the ash from my stove?

Remove ash regularly before it builds up enough to block air flow beneath the grate — for daily use, this typically means every few days. A thick layer of ash smothers the fire and prevents proper burning, while also increasing risk if hot coals are buried within. Leave only a thin layer on the bottom to protect the grate.
My drawknife blade keeps catching and tearing the grain instead of peeling smooth curls. What am I doing wrong?

You are likely working against the grain direction or holding the blade at too steep an angle. Find the grain direction by testing a small area, then draw the blade with the grain at a shallow angle, letting the bevel ride along the wood. Keep the edge sharp and take thinner cuts until the wood cooperates.
My grindstone has worn unevenly and now has a hollow in the middle. How do I flatten it?

Dress the stone by turning it while holding a flat piece of sandstone or a star-drill against the surface, working slowly to remove the high spots. Another method is to rub two worn grindstones face-to-face with sand and water between them, though this requires patience and frequent checking with a straightedge.
The wooden teeth on my hay rake keep breaking off at the socket when they hit stones. Is ash strong enough or should I use something else?

Ash is excellent for rake teeth, but they must have grain running lengthwise without runout at the socket. Splits or cross-grain near the base will always fail under shock. Shape them overlong and cut the socket end from the straightest section.
My knife sharpens well on the stone but the edge rolls over and dulls almost immediately when I use it. What causes this?

You're likely raising a wire edge without removing it, or the final angle is too thin for the steel and purpose. Finish sharpening with lighter strokes on each side to refine the edge, then strop on leather or wood to remove any remaining burr. A slightly thicker edge will hold longer for heavy work than a razor-thin one.
I'm cutting boards with a handsaw and the blade keeps binding and sticking partway through each cut, making the work exhausting.

The set of the teeth may be insufficient, or you may be forcing the cut rather than letting the saw do the work with steady, full strokes. Check that the teeth are properly set to create clearance wider than the blade, and maintain a straight line without twisting. If the wood is green or resinous, occasional binding is natural—withdraw and clear the kerf as needed.
My ladder has one rung that wobbles a bit when I step on it. Is this a problem?

Yes, do not use that ladder until the rung is properly repaired or replaced. A loose rung can give way suddenly under your weight, causing a dangerous fall. Check all the other rungs and joints as well, since weakness in one spot often means others are failing too.
I need to fell a large oak leaning toward the barn. Should I notch the side facing the barn or the opposite side?

Cut your notch on the side you want the tree to fall toward — away from the barn — then make your back cut from the opposite side slightly higher. If the lean is too strong toward the barn, use ropes and a team to pull it safely in the desired direction, or seek experienced help.
My splitting maul keeps bouncing off rounds instead of biting. What's wrong?

A maul that bounces has lost its edge entirely and become too blunt to wedge the wood fibers apart. Take it to the grindstone and restore a proper taper—not razor-sharp like an axe, but a definite edge of about twenty degrees. A truly dull maul makes splitting harder and more dangerous because glancing blows can fly unpredictably.
When driving a chisel with a mallet, where exactly on the handle should I strike?

Strike squarely on the top end of the handle where it is designed to receive blows—this distributes force down the length of the tool properly. Hitting the handle at an angle or partway down causes uneven stress that can split the wood or damage the tang. Keep the mallet face flat and centered with each strike.
I'm sharpening a gouge on the grindstone but the edge keeps coming out uneven no matter how I hold it.

Gouges require a rolling motion to sharpen the curve evenly — rotate the tool steadily while holding the bevel flat against the stone. Practice the motion slowly without pressure first, and keep the stone wet to prevent overheating the thin edge.
My chisel edge is rounded over from too much grinding. Can I just keep using it or should I fix it?

A rounded bevel will not cut cleanly and forces you to apply excessive pressure, risking slips and injury. Regrind the edge to restore the proper angle, checking frequently against a template or known good tool. A properly shaped edge cuts with control and requires far less force.
The wheel on my cart wobbles badly, and I can see the spokes have come loose in the hub. What should I do?

Loose spokes make the wheel unsafe and will worsen rapidly under load. The wheel needs proper repair by driving the spokes tight and possibly shrinking a new iron tire onto the rim. Do not use the cart until the wheel is sound or replaced.
The wooden handle of my hammer has come loose in the head. How should I fix this?

Remove the handle, check both it and the eye of the head for damage, then fit it anew with a proper taper and drive a hardwood wedge firmly into the top end. If the handle has worn thin or split, shape a new one rather than trusting a weakened piece.
I found an old chisel with rust pitting along the edge. How much can I grind away?

Light surface rust can be removed, but deep pitting that reaches the cutting edge weakens the tool. Grind only until you reach sound metal with a smooth bevel; if the pits go so deep that the chisel becomes too short or thin to hold an edge, the tool is spent and should be retired. A pitted edge will always have weak spots that chip or crack under pressure.
When sawing thick timber, my saw keeps wandering off the line no matter how carefully I start the cut. What causes this?

A saw that wanders usually has uneven set in the teeth, meaning one side cuts more aggressively than the other. Check that the teeth are set equally on both sides, and sharpen them to the same size and angle. A saw with proper set and sharp, even teeth will follow your line with only light guidance.
The ladder I use to reach the roof has one rung that feels slightly loose when I step on it.

Do not use that ladder until the rung is properly repaired or replaced. A loose rung can give way entirely under your weight, and even slight movement means the joint has failed. Check all other rungs for soundness and examine the rails for cracks before trusting the ladder again.
My chisel edge has gone rounded and soft. The steel won't hold a line anymore even after I sharpen it.

The edge has lost its temper from overheating, likely on the grindstone. You cannot restore it by sharpening alone; the steel must be re-hardened and re-tempered by heating to cherry red, quenching, then drawing back to straw color. If you lack forge and skill for this, take it to someone who can properly heat-treat the tool.
I need to cut mortises for door hinges but my chisel edge crumbles instead of cutting clean. What am I doing wrong?

Your chisel has lost its temper from overheating during sharpening, making the edge too soft to hold up. You'll need to replace this chisel, as ruined temper cannot be restored with ordinary tools. When sharpening, keep the blade cool by dipping frequently in water and never grinding so fast that the metal blues or changes color.
When I use my drawknife the blade digs in too deep on one side and skips on the other. Am I holding it wrong?

You're likely canting the blade so one corner bites while the other lifts. Keep the edge square to the work and use even pressure on both handles. Draw the knife toward you with your arms moving together, and adjust your body position rather than twisting your wrists to follow the curve of the work.
I'm cutting timber with a crosscut saw and it keeps binding and sticking in the cut. What am I doing wrong?

Ensure the saw teeth have proper set so the cut is wider than the blade thickness. Check that you're cutting straight without twisting, and consider wedging the cut open behind the blade if the timber is settling closed as you work.
The grindstone wobbles when I turn it. Does that matter much?

A wobbling stone will grind unevenly and may shatter if the wobble worsens, sending fragments flying. Check that the axle is straight, the bearings are sound, and the stone is properly centered and secured. If the stone itself is cracked or the mounting hole worn oval, replace it before someone is injured.
My saw cuts crooked no matter how carefully I guide it. What am I doing wrong?

A saw that wanders is usually improperly set—the teeth need even outward bend to cut a clean path, or the blade may have taken a curve from bending. Check that teeth are uniformly sharp and set, and sight down the blade edge to find any twist or bow that wants straightening. Proper maintenance keeps the tool true to your hand.
My hatchet head keeps working loose from the handle when I split kindling. I've tried wedging it tighter but it comes loose again after a few days of use.

The wood of the handle has likely dried and shrunk since fitting. Soak the head in a bucket of water overnight so the wood swells tight again, then drive in a proper wooden or metal wedge while it's wet. Keep the tool stored somewhere with modest moisture rather than near the stove where heat will dry it excessively.
When I'm planing a board, the shavings come out thick on one edge and thin on the other. What am I doing wrong?

You are likely applying uneven pressure or holding the plane askew to the board's face. Keep both hands bearing down equally and sight along the sole to ensure it travels parallel to the work. Check also that the blade projects evenly across its width—a blade set deeper on one side will cut a tapered shaving.
I need to cut mortises in green oak beams. Should I sharpen my chisel differently than for dry wood?

Green oak is softer and more forgiving, so a slightly less acute bevel—perhaps twenty-five degrees instead of twenty—will give you a stronger edge that resists folding. The edge need not be polished to a mirror finish as with cabinetwork; a fine stone will suffice. Keep the bevel flat and true, and clear shavings frequently as the wet wood compacts easily.
My ladder has a cracked rung about halfway up. Should I just avoid stepping on that one?

Replace the cracked rung before using the ladder again. Climbing past a damaged rung puts uneven stress on the rails and remaining rungs, and you may step on it by habit or in haste. A ladder is only as strong as its weakest part.
The wheel on my cart is loose and clatters. Can I drive a few more nails into the hub to tighten it?

Nails will not properly secure a wheel and will split the wood further as it works under load. Remove the wheel and inspect the hub and axle—the hub may need a new iron band shrunk on, or the axle may be worn and need replacement. A wheel that comes off while the cart is moving or loaded is very dangerous.
